questions.subject: government
questions.topic: Arms of government and legislative powers
questions.stem: Under section 48 of the 1999 Constitution, how many Senators make up the Senate of the Federal Republic of Nigeria?

options.text: Three Senators from each State and one from the Federal Capital Territory, Abuja
options.why: Section 48 provides three Senators from each of the 36 States and one from the FCT (109 Senators in total).

options.text: Two Senators from each State and two from the Federal Capital Territory, Abuja
options.why: Each State elects three Senators, not two, while the FCT has one Senator under section 48.
options.whyWrong: Each State elects three Senators, not two, while the FCT has one Senator under section 48.

options.text: Three Senators from each State and three from the Federal Capital Territory, Abuja
options.why: The FCT is represented by one Senator under section 48, not three.
options.whyWrong: The FCT is represented by one Senator under section 48, not three.

options.text: One Senator from each Local Government Area in the Federation
options.why: Senators represent Senatorial districts (three per State), whereas 774 represents Local Government Areas and Area Councils.
options.whyWrong: Senators represent Senatorial districts (three per State), whereas 774 represents Local Government Areas and Area Councils.

questions.hint: Count three Senators per State plus one for the Federal Capital Territory.
questions.explanation: Section 48 of the 1999 Constitution specifies three Senators from each State and one from the Federal Capital Territory, Abuja, giving 109 Senators across the 36 States and FCT.
questions.trap: Students sometimes assume the FCT receives three Senators like a State; section 48 grants the FCT one Senator.
questions.mnemonic: Three per State plus one for the FCT equals 109 Senators.

askPresets.answer: Section 48 of the 1999 Constitution specifies three Senators from each State and one from the Federal Capital Territory, Abuja, giving 109 Senators across the 36 States and FCT.
The FCT is represented by one Senator under section 48, not three.

questions.stem: Section 49 of the 1999 Constitution fixes the total membership of the House of Representatives at

options.text: 109 members
options.why: 109 is the total membership of the Senate under section 48, not the House of Representatives.
options.whyWrong: 109 is the total membership of the Senate under section 48, not the House of Representatives.

options.text: 774 members
options.why: 774 is the total number of Local Government Areas and FCT Area Councils under section 3(6).
options.whyWrong: 774 is the total number of Local Government Areas and FCT Area Councils under section 3(6).

options.text: 469 members
options.why: 469 is the combined total of both Houses of the National Assembly (109 Senators plus 360 Representatives).
options.whyWrong: 469 is the combined total of both Houses of the National Assembly (109 Senators plus 360 Representatives).

options.text: 360 members
options.why: Section 49 provides 360 members representing Federal constituencies of nearly equal population.

questions.hint: Do not add the Senate seats to the lower chamber seats.
questions.explanation: Under section 49 of the 1999 Constitution, the House of Representatives consists of 360 members representing single-member Federal constituencies, with no constituency crossing State boundaries.
questions.trap: 469 is the combined size of the whole National Assembly, which traps students who forget the question asks only for the House of Representatives.
questions.mnemonic: Senate has 109; House of Representatives has 360.

askPresets.answer: Under section 49 of the 1999 Constitution, the House of Representatives consists of 360 members representing single-member Federal constituencies, with no constituency crossing State boundaries.
469 is the combined total of both Houses of the National Assembly (109 Senators plus 360 Representatives).

questions.subject: government
questions.topic: Arms of government and checks and balances
questions.stem: When an ordinary bill is presented to the President for assent under section 58(4) of the 1999 Constitution, within how many days must the President signify assent or withhold it?

options.text: 14 days
options.why: 14 days applies to Joint Finance Committee convening (s. 59(2)) or impeachment resolution timelines (s. 143(3)), not general bill assent.
options.whyWrong: 14 days applies to Joint Finance Committee convening (s. 59(2)) or impeachment resolution timelines (s. 143(3)), not general bill assent.

options.text: 30 days
options.why: Section 58(4) gives the President 30 days from presentation to signify assent or withhold assent.

options.text: 21 days
options.why: 21 days is the deadline to file an election petition (s. 285(5)) or transfer foreign party funds (s. 225(4)), not presidential assent.
options.whyWrong: 21 days is the deadline to file an election petition (s. 285(5)) or transfer foreign party funds (s. 225(4)), not presidential assent.

options.text: 60 days
options.why: 60 days is the deadline for appellate election judgments (s. 285(7)) or ministerial nomination after oath (s. 147(7)), not bill assent.
options.whyWrong: 60 days is the deadline for appellate election judgments (s. 285(7)) or ministerial nomination after oath (s. 147(7)), not bill assent.

questions.hint: Think of one standard month for the President to review a passed bill.
questions.explanation: Under section 58(4) of the 1999 Constitution, the President has 30 days after receiving a bill from the National Assembly to assent or withhold assent.
questions.trap: Students frequently confuse the 21-day window for Senate confirmation deemed-approval (s. 147(6)) with the 30-day window for presidential assent to bills.
questions.mnemonic: Thirty days to sign or decline a bill under section 58.

askPresets.answer: Under section 58(4) of the 1999 Constitution, the President has 30 days after receiving a bill from the National Assembly to assent or withhold assent.
21 days is the deadline to file an election petition (s. 285(5)) or transfer foreign party funds (s. 225(4)), not presidential assent.

questions.subject: government
questions.topic: Arms of government and checks and balances
questions.stem: If the President withholds assent to a bill passed by the National Assembly, how can the National Assembly override the veto under section 58(5)?

options.text: By a simple majority of members present in the House of Representatives alone
options.why: A veto override requires both Houses and a two-thirds supermajority, not one House or a simple majority.
options.whyWrong: A veto override requires both Houses and a two-thirds supermajority, not one House or a simple majority.

options.text: By obtaining approval from a majority of State Houses of Assembly
options.why: State Houses of Assembly ratify constitutional alterations (s. 9) or certain treaties (s. 12(3)), not ordinary bill veto overrides.
options.whyWrong: State Houses of Assembly ratify constitutional alterations (s. 9) or certain treaties (s. 12(3)), not ordinary bill veto overrides.

options.text: By passing the bill again in each House by a two-thirds majority
options.why: Section 58(5) states that if each House passes the bill again by a two-thirds majority, it becomes law without presidential assent.

options.text: By referring the bill to the Supreme Court for signature
options.why: The Supreme Court interprets laws and settles disputes; it never signs or enacts bills.
options.whyWrong: The Supreme Court interprets laws and settles disputes; it never signs or enacts bills.

questions.hint: Ask what legislative supermajority forces an ordinary bill into law without the President's signature.
questions.explanation: Under section 58(5), where the President withholds assent and the bill is again passed by each House of the National Assembly by a two-thirds majority, the bill becomes law without presidential assent.
questions.trap: Some candidates mix up ordinary veto override (two-thirds of each House alone) with constitutional alteration (which also needs State Houses of Assembly).
questions.mnemonic: Two-thirds in each House overrides a presidential veto.

askPresets.answer: Under section 58(5), where the President withholds assent and the bill is again passed by each House of the National Assembly by a two-thirds majority, the bill becomes law without presidential assent.
State Houses of Assembly ratify constitutional alterations (s. 9) or certain treaties (s. 12(3)), not ordinary bill veto overrides.

questions.subject: government
questions.topic: Arms of government and legislative powers
questions.stem: Under section 54(1) and (1A) of the 1999 Constitution, what is the quorum for an ordinary sitting of the Senate compared with its inaugural first sitting?

options.text: One-half for ordinary sittings, and simple majority for inaugural sittings
options.why: Ordinary sittings require one-third, not one-half, and inaugural sittings require at least two-thirds.
options.whyWrong: Ordinary sittings require one-third, not one-half, and inaugural sittings require at least two-thirds.

options.text: Two-thirds of all members for ordinary sittings, and one-third for inaugural sittings
options.why: This reverses the two thresholds in section 54(1) and (1A).
options.whyWrong: This reverses the two thresholds in section 54(1) and (1A).

options.text: One-third of all members for ordinary sittings, and at least two-thirds of members-elect for inaugural sittings
options.why: Section 54(1) sets the ordinary quorum at one-third of all members, while section 54(1A) sets inaugural and first sittings at two-thirds.

options.text: One-quarter of all members for ordinary sittings, and one-half for inaugural sittings
options.why: One-quarter applies to State vote spread in presidential elections, not legislative quorums.
options.whyWrong: One-quarter applies to State vote spread in presidential elections, not legislative quorums.

questions.hint: A brand-new Assembly electing its presiding officers needs a higher attendance than a routine workday.
questions.explanation: Section 54(1) fixes the normal quorum of either House at one-third of all its members, whereas section 54(1A) requires at least two-thirds of all members-elect for the inaugural and first sitting.
questions.trap: Reversing the two fractions is the classic trap here; inaugural sittings demand the stricter two-thirds quorum.
questions.mnemonic: One-third for daily work; two-thirds to start a new Assembly.

askPresets.answer: Section 54(1) fixes the normal quorum of either House at one-third of all its members, whereas section 54(1A) requires at least two-thirds of all members-elect for the inaugural and first sitting.
This reverses the two thresholds in section 54(1) and (1A).

questions.concept: Money bills and Joint Finance Committee
questions.stem: Under section 59(2)–(3) of the 1999 Constitution, if one House passes an Appropriation Bill and the other House fails to pass it within two months from the start of the financial year, what is the next constitutional step?

options.text: The President of the Senate convenes a Joint Finance Committee within 14 days, and if unresolved, a joint meeting of the National Assembly
options.why: Section 59(2)–(3) directs the Senate President to convene a Joint Finance Committee within 14 days, followed by a joint sitting if needed.

options.text: The President signs the version passed by the first House immediately
options.why: The President cannot sign a money bill passed by only one House without resolving differences between both chambers.
options.whyWrong: The President cannot sign a money bill passed by only one House without resolving differences between both chambers.

options.text: The bill lapses permanently until the following financial year
options.why: The Constitution provides a deadlock-breaking mechanism for money bills rather than letting the budget lapse.
options.whyWrong: The Constitution provides a deadlock-breaking mechanism for money bills rather than letting the budget lapse.

options.text: The Supreme Court resolves the budget figures for both Houses
options.why: Budget deadlocks are legislative matters resolved inside the National Assembly under section 59, not by courts.
options.whyWrong: Budget deadlocks are legislative matters resolved inside the National Assembly under section 59, not by courts.

questions.hint: Look for the special two-chamber committee designed specifically for money bills.
questions.explanation: Under section 59(2)–(3), if a money bill stalls in the second House for two months, the Senate President convenes the Joint Finance Committee within 14 days; if differences persist, both Houses vote on it in a joint sitting.
questions.trap: Students sometimes think the President can assent to a single-chamber budget bill, whereas section 59 requires joint legislative resolution first.
questions.mnemonic: Money deadlock goes to Joint Finance Committee, then Joint Sitting.

askPresets.answer: Under section 59(2)–(3), if a money bill stalls in the second House for two months, the Senate President convenes the Joint Finance Committee within 14 days; if differences persist, both Houses vote on it in a joint sitting.
The President cannot sign a money bill passed by only one House without resolving differences between both chambers.

questions.subject: government
questions.topic: Arms of government and separation of powers
questions.stem: A serving member of the House of Representatives is nominated as a Federal Minister, confirmed by the Senate, and takes the oath of office as Minister. Under section 147(4), what happens to the legislative seat?

options.text: The member is deemed to have resigned membership of the House of Representatives
options.why: Section 147(4) and section 68(1)(d) make resignation from the legislative house automatic upon taking the ministerial oath.

options.text: The member holds both seats so the executive can answer questions directly in the House
options.why: Dual membership in cabinet and parliament belongs to a parliamentary system, which Nigeria's presidential constitution forbids.
options.whyWrong: Dual membership in cabinet and parliament belongs to a parliamentary system, which Nigeria's presidential constitution forbids.

options.text: The member takes unpaid leave from the House until the ministerial appointment ends
options.why: The seat becomes vacant permanently and must be filled by by-election, rather than remaining on leave.
options.whyWrong: The seat becomes vacant permanently and must be filled by by-election, rather than remaining on leave.

options.text: The member keeps the House seat only if the political party approves
options.why: Constitutional separation of personnel under section 147(4) overrides internal party preferences.
options.whyWrong: Constitutional separation of personnel under section 147(4) overrides internal party preferences.

questions.hint: Remember how Nigeria's presidential constitution separates the personnel of the executive and legislature.
questions.explanation: Under section 147(4) (and section 68(1)(d)) of the 1999 Constitution, any member of the National Assembly or a State House of Assembly appointed as a Federal Minister is deemed to have resigned from the legislature upon taking the oath of office.
questions.trap: Because British-style parliamentary ministers sit in parliament, candidates often pick dual membership by mistake.
questions.mnemonic: Take a Minister's oath, leave your legislative seat.

askPresets.answer: Under section 147(4) (and section 68(1)(d)) of the 1999 Constitution, any member of the National Assembly or a State House of Assembly appointed as a Federal Minister is deemed to have resigned from the legislature upon taking the oath of office.
Dual membership in cabinet and parliament belongs to a parliamentary system, which Nigeria's presidential constitution forbids.

questions.subject: government
questions.topic: Arms of government and executive powers
questions.stem: Which constitutional rule governs the appointment of Federal Ministers under section 147 of the 1999 Constitution (as amended by the Fifth Alteration)?

options.text: The House of Representatives confirms Ministers without Senate involvement
options.why: Ministerial confirmation belongs solely to the Senate under section 147(2), not the House of Representatives.
options.whyWrong: Ministerial confirmation belongs solely to the Senate under section 147(2), not the House of Representatives.

options.text: The President must nominate Ministers within 60 days of taking the oath of office, and the Senate must confirm them
options.why: Section 147(2) requires Senate confirmation (with evidence of asset declaration), and section 147(7) sets a 60-day window from the President's oath.

options.text: The President may appoint all Ministers from a single geopolitical zone
options.why: Section 147(3) requires compliance with section 14(3) and mandates at least one Minister who is an indigene of each State.
options.whyWrong: Section 147(3) requires compliance with section 14(3) and mandates at least one Minister who is an indigene of each State.

options.text: The Chief Justice of Nigeria approves all ministerial nominees before Senate screening
options.why: The Chief Justice has no role in approving ministerial nominees; screening and confirmation rest with the Senate.
options.whyWrong: The Chief Justice has no role in approving ministerial nominees; screening and confirmation rest with the Senate.

questions.hint: Check which chamber screens federal nominees and the 60-day timeline added by the Fifth Alteration.
questions.explanation: Section 147(2) requires Senate confirmation (with asset declaration evidence) for Ministerial appointments, s. 147(3) requires at least one indigene Minister per State, and s. 147(7) (Fifth Alteration No. 23, 2023) requires initial nominations within 60 days of taking the presidential oath.
questions.trap: Candidates sometimes guess the House of Representatives or the whole National Assembly confirms Ministers, whereas only the Senate holds confirmation power.
questions.mnemonic: Senate confirms Ministers; one indigene per State; nominate within 60 days.

askPresets.answer: Section 147(2) requires Senate confirmation (with asset declaration evidence) for Ministerial appointments, s. 147(3) requires at least one indigene Minister per State, and s. 147(7) (Fifth Alteration No. 23, 2023) requires initial nominations within 60 days of taking the presidential oath.
Ministerial confirmation belongs solely to the Senate under section 147(2), not the House of Representatives.

questions.subject: government
questions.topic: Arms of government and checks and balances
questions.stem: If the President is unable to discharge the functions of office and fails to transmit a written declaration within 21 days, what does section 145(2) empower the National Assembly to do?

options.text: Remove the President immediately for gross misconduct
options.why: Temporary inability is distinct from gross-misconduct impeachment under section 143.
options.whyWrong: Temporary inability is distinct from gross-misconduct impeachment under section 143.

options.text: Pass a resolution by a simple majority of each House mandating the Vice-President to act as Acting President
options.why: Section 145(2) (First Alteration, 2010) empowers both Houses by simple majority resolution to mandate the Vice-President as Acting President until the President transmits a resumption letter.

options.text: Appoint the Senate President as Acting President automatically
options.why: The Senate President acts only when both President and Vice-President offices are vacant or incapacitated under section 146, not under section 145.
options.whyWrong: The Senate President acts only when both President and Vice-President offices are vacant or incapacitated under section 146, not under section 145.

options.text: Ask the Supreme Court to declare the Presidency vacant
options.why: Temporary absence under section 145 is handled by a legislative resolution empowering the Vice-President, not by court removal.
options.whyWrong: Temporary absence under section 145 is handled by a legislative resolution empowering the Vice-President, not by court removal.

questions.hint: Who steps in first when the President is temporarily unable to act?
questions.explanation: Inserted by the First Alteration (2010), section 145(2) provides that if the President does not transmit a vacation or inability declaration within 21 days, the National Assembly may by simple majority resolution of each House mandate the Vice-President to perform the functions as Acting President.
questions.trap: Students often confuse section 145 (temporary absence, Vice-President acts) with section 146(2) (vacancy of both President and Vice-President, Senate President acts for 3 months).
questions.mnemonic: 21 days without a letter lets Parliament empower the Vice-President.

askPresets.answer: Inserted by the First Alteration (2010), section 145(2) provides that if the President does not transmit a vacation or inability declaration within 21 days, the National Assembly may by simple majority resolution of each House mandate the Vice-President to perform the functions as Acting President.
The Senate President acts only when both President and Vice-President offices are vacant or incapacitated under section 146, not under section 145.

questions.subject: government
questions.topic: Arms of government and checks and balances
questions.stem: During impeachment proceedings against the President under section 143(5) of the 1999 Constitution, who appoints the seven-person investigative panel?

options.text: The President of the Senate, acting on the advice of the Attorney-General
options.why: The Senate President requests the appointment, while the Chief Justice actually appoints the panel.
options.whyWrong: The Senate President requests the appointment, while the Chief Justice actually appoints the panel.

options.text: The Vice-President, in consultation with State Governors
options.why: The Vice-President has no constitutional role in appointing an impeachment panel.
options.whyWrong: The Vice-President has no constitutional role in appointing an impeachment panel.

options.text: The Chief Justice of Nigeria, at the request of the President of the Senate
options.why: Section 143(5) directs the Chief Justice of Nigeria to appoint seven persons of unquestionable integrity within seven days of the two-thirds motion.

options.text: The Speaker of the House of Representatives alone
options.why: The Speaker notifies and presides in the House, whereas section 143(5) assigns panel appointment to the Chief Justice of Nigeria.
options.whyWrong: The Speaker notifies and presides in the House, whereas section 143(5) assigns panel appointment to the Chief Justice of Nigeria.

questions.hint: Notice how a neutral judicial head selects the investigators once lawmakers pass the investigation motion.
questions.explanation: Under section 143(5), within seven days of both Houses passing a two-thirds motion to investigate gross misconduct allegations, the Chief Justice of Nigeria appoints a panel of seven persons of unquestionable integrity who belong to no public service, legislative house, or political party.
questions.trap: Because the Senate President receives the notice and requests the panel, students often assume the Senate President picks the seven members directly.
questions.mnemonic: Senate President requests; Chief Justice appoints the 7-person panel.

askPresets.answer: Under section 143(5), within seven days of both Houses passing a two-thirds motion to investigate gross misconduct allegations, the Chief Justice of Nigeria appoints a panel of seven persons of unquestionable integrity who belong to no public service, legislative house, or political party.
The Senate President requests the appointment, while the Chief Justice actually appoints the panel.

questions.subject: government
questions.topic: Arms of government and checks and balances
questions.concept: Final impeachment vote and court bar
questions.stem: In presidential removal proceedings under section 143(8)–(10), if the seven-person panel reports that the allegation has been proved, what happens next?

options.text: The Supreme Court conducts a full retrial before removal takes effect
options.why: Section 143(10) explicitly bars any court from entertaining or questioning the proceedings or determination of the panel or National Assembly.
options.whyWrong: Section 143(10) explicitly bars any court from entertaining or questioning the proceedings or determination of the panel or National Assembly.

options.text: A simple majority of the House of Representatives alone removes the President
options.why: Both Houses must adopt the panel's report by at least a two-thirds majority of all their members.
options.whyWrong: Both Houses must adopt the panel's report by at least a two-thirds majority of all their members.

options.text: Each House considers the report within 14 days, and adoption by a two-thirds majority of all members of each House removes the holder
options.why: Section 143(9) provides for removal upon adoption of the proved report by two-thirds of all members of each House within 14 days.

options.text: The panel itself issues a binding removal order without returning to Parliament
options.why: The panel reports its findings back to each House, which votes on adoption under section 143(9).
options.whyWrong: The panel reports its findings back to each House, which votes on adoption under section 143(9).

questions.hint: Check who takes the final vote after the panel finishes investigating.
questions.explanation: Under section 143(9), if the panel reports the allegation proved, each House has 14 days to consider it; if each House adopts it by not less than a two-thirds majority of all its members, the holder stands removed, and section 143(10) bars court questioning.
questions.trap: Many candidates expect a final appeal to the Supreme Court, overlooking the ouster clause in section 143(10).
questions.mnemonic: Two-thirds to investigate, seven-person panel, two-thirds of each House to remove.

askPresets.answer: Under section 143(9), if the panel reports the allegation proved, each House has 14 days to consider it; if each House adopts it by not less than a two-thirds majority of all its members, the holder stands removed, and section 143(10) bars court questioning.
Section 143(10) explicitly bars any court from entertaining or questioning the proceedings or determination of the panel or National Assembly.

questions.stem: Under section 88(2) of the 1999 Constitution, the National Assembly may conduct investigations into executive ministries and agencies strictly for the purpose of

options.text: making or correcting laws within its competence and exposing corruption, inefficiency or waste
options.why: Section 88(2)(a)–(b) restricts legislative investigations to lawmaking/defect correction and exposing corruption, inefficiency, or waste in law execution or fund disbursement.

options.text: replacing the courts in convicting and jailing corrupt officials
options.why: Convicting and sentencing offenders belongs to the judiciary under section 6, not legislative committees.
options.whyWrong: Convicting and sentencing offenders belongs to the judiciary under section 6, not legislative committees.

options.text: appointing permanent secretaries and ambassadors directly
options.why: Public service and ambassadorial appointments belong to the executive (with Senate confirmation for ambassadors under s. 171(4)).
options.whyWrong: Public service and ambassadorial appointments belong to the executive (with Senate confirmation for ambassadors under s. 171(4)).

options.text: overturning Supreme Court judgments on election petitions
options.why: Legislative investigations cannot reverse judicial decisions.
options.whyWrong: Legislative investigations cannot reverse judicial decisions.

questions.hint: Think about why lawmakers investigate rather than prosecute or judge.
questions.explanation: Section 88(2) limits the National Assembly's investigative powers to enabling it to make or correct laws within its legislative competence and exposing corruption, inefficiency, or waste in administering its laws and appropriated funds.
questions.trap: Because investigations uncover wrongdoing, students sometimes pick criminal conviction, which only courts can pronounce.
questions.mnemonic: Lawmakers investigate to legislate and expose waste, not to convict.

askPresets.answer: Section 88(2) limits the National Assembly's investigative powers to enabling it to make or correct laws within its legislative competence and exposing corruption, inefficiency, or waste in administering its laws and appropriated funds.
Convicting and sentencing offenders belongs to the judiciary under section 6, not legislative committees.

questions.subject: government
questions.concept: Judicial review and ban on ouster clauses
questions.stem: Which constitutional provision guarantees that the National Assembly or a State House of Assembly cannot enact a law stopping courts from reviewing legislative acts?

options.text: Section 58(5), which governs presidential veto overrides
options.why: Section 58(5) deals with overriding a presidential veto, not judicial review.
options.whyWrong: Section 58(5) deals with overriding a presidential veto, not judicial review.

options.text: Section 143(10), which protects impeachment votes
options.why: Section 143(10) is a specific exception barring court review of impeachment proceedings, not a general ban on ouster clauses.
options.whyWrong: Section 143(10) is a specific exception barring court review of impeachment proceedings, not a general ban on ouster clauses.

options.text: Section 6(6)(c), which covers Chapter II Directive Principles
options.why: Section 6(6)(c) limits judicial power over Chapter II Directive Principles rather than stopping lawmakers from ousting courts.
options.whyWrong: Section 6(6)(c) limits judicial power over Chapter II Directive Principles rather than stopping lawmakers from ousting courts.

options.text: Section 4(8), which subjects legislative power to court jurisdiction and forbids ouster clauses
options.why: Section 4(8) forbids both the National Assembly and State Houses of Assembly from enacting laws that oust court jurisdiction.

questions.hint: Look inside section 4 (legislative powers) for the subsection that protects the courts.
questions.explanation: Section 4(8) states that the exercise of legislative powers by the National Assembly or a House of Assembly is subject to the jurisdiction of courts and tribunals, and neither may enact any law that ousts court jurisdiction.
questions.trap: Candidates sometimes confuse s. 4(8) (ban on ouster clauses) with s. 6(6)(c) (non-justiciability of Chapter II).
questions.mnemonic: Section 4(8) keeps the courtroom doors open against ouster laws.

askPresets.answer: Section 4(8) states that the exercise of legislative powers by the National Assembly or a House of Assembly is subject to the jurisdiction of courts and tribunals, and neither may enact any law that ousts court jurisdiction.
Section 6(6)(c) limits judicial power over Chapter II Directive Principles rather than stopping lawmakers from ousting courts.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Under section 238(1)–(2) of the 1999 Constitution, what is the difference between appointing the President of the Court of Appeal and appointing other Justices of the Court of Appeal?

options.text: Both require confirmation by the House of Representatives
options.why: The House of Representatives has no constitutional role in confirming judicial appointments.
options.whyWrong: The House of Representatives has no constitutional role in confirming judicial appointments.

options.text: Other Justices require Senate confirmation, while the President of the Court of Appeal does not
options.why: This reverses subsections (1) and (2) of section 238.
options.whyWrong: This reverses subsections (1) and (2) of section 238.

options.text: Neither office requires any recommendation from the National Judicial Council
options.why: Both appointments require recommendation by the National Judicial Council under section 238(1)–(2).
options.whyWrong: Both appointments require recommendation by the National Judicial Council under section 238(1)–(2).

options.text: Only the President of the Court of Appeal requires Senate confirmation in addition to National Judicial Council recommendation
options.why: Under s. 238(1), the President of the Court of Appeal is appointed by the President on NJC recommendation subject to Senate confirmation, whereas s. 238(2) omits Senate confirmation for other Justices of the Court of Appeal.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Why is Nigeria's 1999 Constitution classified as a written constitution?

options.text: Because parliamentary speeches are recorded in Hansard
options.why: Recording parliamentary debates does not make a constitution written.
options.whyWrong: Recording parliamentary debates does not make a constitution written.

options.text: Because its fundamental rules on institutions, powers and rights are codified in one formal document
options.why: A written constitution sets out the structure of government, powers, and citizens' rights in a single codified document (Preamble, Chapters I–VIII, and Schedules).

options.text: Because laws can only be written in English and never translated
options.why: Codification into a single supreme text — not the language used — defines a written constitution.
options.whyWrong: Codification into a single supreme text — not the language used — defines a written constitution.

options.whyWrong: Ease of amendment defines flexibility, not whether a constitution is written.

questions.explanation: A written constitution (such as Nigeria's 1999 Constitution) brings the fundamental rules defining government organs, their powers, and citizens' rights together into one codified legal document.

options.whyWrong: Length in sections does not determine rigidity; amendment procedure does.

options.text: Whether the armed forces enforce constitutional provisions

options.text: disciplining an employee who arrives late to work

questions.stem: Under section 35(2)–(3) of the 1999 Constitution, a person arrested or detained is entitled to remain silent until consulting a legal practitioner and must be informed of the grounds for arrest in writing within

options.text: 24 hours, in a language the person understands

options.text: 72 hours, in English only

options.whyWrong: The time limit is 24 hours, not 72 hours, and the language must be one the suspect understands.

options.text: 14 days, if the person has no lawyer

options.whyWrong: Lack of a lawyer never extends the 24-hour written notice duty.

questions.explanation: Section 35(2) protects the right to remain silent until consulting a lawyer or person of choice, and section 35(3) requires written notice of arrest facts and grounds within 24 hours in a language the suspect understands.

questions.stem: A suspect is arrested on suspicion of theft in a rural town where the nearest competent court is 90 kilometres away. Under section 35(5)(b), what constitutes 'a reasonable time' to bring the suspect before a court?

options.text: A period of 2 days, or such longer period as the court considers reasonable in the circumstances
options.why: Under s. 35(5)(b), where no competent court sits within 40 km, a reasonable time is 2 days or such longer period as the court deems reasonable.

options.text: A period of 1 day strictly
options.why: 1 day applies under s. 35(5)(a) only when a competent court is within a 40 km radius.
options.whyWrong: 1 day applies under s. 35(5)(a) only when a competent court is within a 40 km radius.

options.text: A period of 2 months
options.why: 2 months (s. 35(4)(a)) is the limit for trial when held without bail, not first appearance before a court.
options.whyWrong: 2 months (s. 35(4)(a)) is the limit for trial when held without bail, not first appearance before a court.

options.text: A period of 6 months
options.why: No 6-month pre-arraignment window exists in section 35.
options.whyWrong: No 6-month pre-arraignment window exists in section 35.

questions.explanation: Section 35(5) defines 'a reasonable time' to bring an arrested person before a court as 1 day if a competent court lies within 40 km (s. 35(5)(a)), and 2 days (or longer if considered reasonable by the court) in any other case (s. 35(5)(b)).
questions.trap: Students who memorise only '24 hours / 1 day' overlook the 40 km rule in section 35(5)(b).
questions.mnemonic: Within 40 km = 1 day; beyond 40 km = 2 days (or reasonable).

askPresets.answer: Section 35(5) defines 'a reasonable time' to bring an arrested person before a court as 1 day if a competent court lies within 40 km (s. 35(5)(a)), and 2 days (or longer if considered reasonable by the court) in any other case (s. 35(5)(b)).
1 day applies under s. 35(5)(a) only when a competent court is within a 40 km radius.

questions.stem: Which principle in section 36(5) of the 1999 Constitution protects an accused person standing criminal trial?

options.why: Reversing the general burden of proof contradicts the presumption of innocence in section 36(5).
options.whyWrong: Reversing the general burden of proof contradicts the presumption of innocence in section 36(5).

options.text: Every person charged with a criminal offence is presumed innocent until proved guilty
options.why: Section 36(5) enshrines the presumption of innocence until proved guilty (subject to narrow statutory provisos on specific facts).

options.text: Criminal trials must always be held in secret chambers
options.why: Section 36(4) requires criminal trials to be held in public, save narrow exceptions.
options.whyWrong: Section 36(4) requires criminal trials to be held in public, save narrow exceptions.

options.text: An accused person may be tried twice for the same offence if acquitted
options.why: Double jeopardy is barred by section 36(9).
options.whyWrong: Double jeopardy is barred by section 36(9).

questions.mnemonic: Section 36(5): innocent until proved guilty.

options.why: Section 36(10) bars retrial only if pardoned for an offence, not automatic pardon after appeals.
options.whyWrong: Section 36(10) bars retrial only if pardoned for an offence, not automatic pardon after appeals.

options.whyWrong: Fair hearing does not excuse ignoring court summons or erase civil debts.

options.why: Section 36(8) forbids backdated criminal laws or heavier penalties, and s. 36(9) forbids trying a person again after final conviction or acquittal.

options.why: The proviso to s. 39(2) allows private broadcast ownership only if authorised by the President under conditions in an Act of the National Assembly.

questions.stem: During a proclamation of a state of emergency under section 305, what does the proviso to section 45(2) forbid the government from ever doing?

options.text: Curfewing movement in an affected area
options.why: Movement limits can be imposed under s. 45(1) or emergency measures if reasonably justifiable.
options.whyWrong: Movement limits can be imposed under s. 45(1) or emergency measures if reasonably justifiable.

options.text: Derogating from the right to life except for deaths from acts of war, or derogating from section 36(8) against retroactive crimes
options.why: The proviso to s. 45(2) strictly bars any derogation from s. 33 (except acts of war) or from s. 36(8).

options.text: Deploying federal security forces to restore order
options.why: Maintaining public safety during an emergency is the purpose of section 305.
options.whyWrong: Maintaining public safety during an emergency is the purpose of section 305.

options.text: Temporarily adjusting detention periods where reasonably justifiable
options.why: Reasonably justifiable measures under s. 35 are expressly contemplated during a s. 305 emergency.
options.whyWrong: Reasonably justifiable measures under s. 35 are expressly contemplated during a s. 305 emergency.

questions.hint: Check the two absolute red lines in the proviso to section 45(2).
questions.explanation: While section 45(2) allows reasonably justifiable emergency measures affecting ss. 33 or 35, its proviso strictly forbids any derogation from s. 33 except death from acts of war, and forbids any derogation whatsoever from s. 36(8) (retroactive offences/penalties).
questions.trap: Because s. 45(2) mentions s. 33 and s. 35, students often think emergencies suspend the right to life altogether.
questions.mnemonic: Even in emergencies: no non-war killing, no backdated crimes.

askPresets.answer: While section 45(2) allows reasonably justifiable emergency measures affecting ss. 33 or 35, its proviso strictly forbids any derogation from s. 33 except death from acts of war, and forbids any derogation whatsoever from s. 36(8) (retroactive offences/penalties).
Reasonably justifiable measures under s. 35 are expressly contemplated during a s. 305 emergency.

questions.concept: Chapter II vs Chapter IV justiciability
questions.stem: Why can a citizen sue in a High Court under section 46 to enforce freedom of expression (s. 39), yet cannot sue directly to compel government to provide free university education (s. 18)?

options.text: Because Chapter II applies only to the Federal Capital Territory
options.why: Chapter II applies across Nigeria as guiding policy directives for all organs of government (s. 13).
options.whyWrong: Chapter II applies across Nigeria as guiding policy directives for all organs of government (s. 13).

options.text: Because education is listed on the Exclusive Legislative List
options.why: Education appears on the Concurrent Legislative List, not as a bar to rights enforcement.
options.whyWrong: Education appears on the Concurrent Legislative List, not as a bar to rights enforcement.

options.text: Because High Courts handle criminal cases only
options.why: High Courts have civil, constitutional, and fundamental-rights jurisdiction under ss. 46, 251, and 272.
options.whyWrong: High Courts have civil, constitutional, and fundamental-rights jurisdiction under ss. 46, 251, and 272.

options.text: Because section 39 is in Chapter IV (Fundamental Rights), whereas section 18 is in Chapter II, which section 6(6)(c) makes non-justiciable
options.why: Section 46 grants High Court redress for Chapter IV rights (ss. 33–46), while s. 6(6)(c) bars courts from enforcing Chapter II Directive Principles (ss. 13–24) directly.

questions.hint: Contrast Chapter II (Directive Principles) with Chapter IV (Fundamental Rights) using section 6(6)(c).
questions.explanation: Section 6(6)(c) excludes judicial enforcement of Chapter II (Fundamental Objectives and Directive Principles, ss. 13–24) unless implemented by legislation, whereas section 46 empowers High Courts to enforce all Chapter IV Fundamental Rights (ss. 33–46) and provides legal aid for indigent citizens.
questions.trap: Students often mistake inspiring social goals in Chapter II for directly enforceable Chapter IV legal rights.
questions.mnemonic: Chapter IV goes to High Court (s. 46); Chapter II guides policy (s. 6(6)(c)).

askPresets.answer: Section 6(6)(c) excludes judicial enforcement of Chapter II (Fundamental Objectives and Directive Principles, ss. 13–24) unless implemented by legislation, whereas section 46 empowers High Courts to enforce all Chapter IV Fundamental Rights (ss. 33–46) and provides legal aid for indigent citizens.
Chapter II applies across Nigeria as guiding policy directives for all organs of government (s. 13).

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Under section 25(1)(a) of the 1999 Constitution, a person born in Nigeria before 1 October 1960 is a citizen of Nigeria by birth if either parent or any grandparent belonged to an indigenous Nigerian community, provided that

options.text: the person has lived continuously in Abuja for 15 years
options.why: 15 years residence is for naturalisation under section 27, not birth under section 25.
options.whyWrong: 15 years residence is for naturalisation under section 27, not birth under section 25.

options.text: at least one of the person's parents or grandparents was born in Nigeria
options.why: The proviso to s. 25(1)(a) requires that at least one parent or grandparent was born in Nigeria.

options.text: the person holds a university degree
options.why: Education is never a requirement for citizenship by birth.
options.whyWrong: Education is never a requirement for citizenship by birth.

options.text: the person has taken the Oath of Allegiance
options.why: Taking the Oath of Allegiance applies to registration (s. 26) and naturalisation (s. 27), not birth.
options.whyWrong: Taking the Oath of Allegiance applies to registration (s. 26) and naturalisation (s. 27), not birth.

questions.hint: Read the proviso attached to section 25(1)(a) carefully.
questions.explanation: Under section 25(1)(a), anyone born in Nigeria before independence (1 October 1960) with a parent or grandparent belonging to a community indigenous to Nigeria is a citizen by birth, provided at least one parent or grandparent was born in Nigeria.
questions.trap: Most candidates remember the indigenous community rule yet overlook the proviso requiring a parent or grandparent born in Nigeria.
questions.mnemonic: Pre-1960 birth: indigenous tie PLUS parent or grandparent born in Nigeria.

askPresets.answer: Under section 25(1)(a), anyone born in Nigeria before independence (1 October 1960) with a parent or grandparent belonging to a community indigenous to Nigeria is a citizen by birth, provided at least one parent or grandparent was born in Nigeria.
Taking the Oath of Allegiance applies to registration (s. 26) and naturalisation (s. 27), not birth.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Two German engineers working temporarily in Port Harcourt have a baby in Port Harcourt in 2010. Neither parent nor any grandparent of the baby is Nigerian. Under section 25, the baby is

options.text: a Nigerian citizen by birth because the birth occurred in Nigeria
options.why: After 1 October 1960, birth on Nigerian soil alone does not grant citizenship without a Nigerian parent or grandparent (s. 25(1)(b)).
options.whyWrong: After 1 October 1960, birth on Nigerian soil alone does not grant citizenship without a Nigerian parent or grandparent (s. 25(1)(b)).

options.text: NOT a Nigerian citizen by birth, because neither parent nor any grandparent is a Nigerian citizen
options.why: Section 25(1)(b) requires birth in Nigeria after independence PLUS at least one Nigerian citizen parent or grandparent.

options.text: a Nigerian citizen by registration automatically
options.why: Registration under s. 26 requires application and applies only to wives of citizens or adult grandchildren of citizens born abroad.
options.whyWrong: Registration under s. 26 requires application and applies only to wives of citizens or adult grandchildren of citizens born abroad.

options.text: a citizen by naturalisation at birth
options.why: Naturalisation (s. 27) requires full age and 15 years residence, never birth.
options.whyWrong: Naturalisation (s. 27) requires full age and 15 years residence, never birth.

questions.hint: Does Nigeria follow pure jus soli (soil alone) or parentage/ancestry after 1960?
questions.explanation: Section 25(1)(b) grants citizenship by birth to persons born in Nigeria after 1 October 1960 only if either parent or any grandparent is a citizen of Nigeria. Birth on Nigerian soil to two non-Nigerians confers no birth citizenship.
questions.trap: Thinking 'born in Nigeria equals Nigerian citizen' is the single biggest trap on section 25.
questions.mnemonic: After 1960: Nigerian soil still needs Nigerian blood (parent or grandparent).

askPresets.answer: Section 25(1)(b) grants citizenship by birth to persons born in Nigeria after 1 October 1960 only if either parent or any grandparent is a citizen of Nigeria. Birth on Nigerian soil to two non-Nigerians confers no birth citizenship.
After 1 October 1960, birth on Nigerian soil alone does not grant citizenship without a Nigerian parent or grandparent (s. 25(1)(b)).

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: A child is born in London in 2015. The mother is a Nigerian citizen, and the father is British. Under section 25(1)(c) of the 1999 Constitution, what is the child's Nigerian citizenship status?

options.text: Citizen of Nigeria by registration only after turning 18
options.why: Registration under s. 26(2)(b) applies when a *grandparent* (not a parent) is a citizen for a child born abroad.
options.whyWrong: Registration under s. 26(2)(b) applies when a *grandparent* (not a parent) is a citizen for a child born abroad.

options.text: Citizen only if both parents are Nigerians
options.why: Section 25(1)(c) says 'either of whose parents' — one Nigerian parent suffices.
options.whyWrong: Section 25(1)(c) says 'either of whose parents' — one Nigerian parent suffices.

options.text: Ineligible unless the child lives in Nigeria for 15 years
options.why: 15 years residence is for naturalisation under s. 27.
options.whyWrong: 15 years residence is for naturalisation under s. 27.

options.text: Citizen of Nigeria by birth because one parent is a citizen of Nigeria
options.why: Section 25(1)(c) confers citizenship by birth on every person born outside Nigeria either of whose parents is a citizen of Nigeria.

questions.hint: Distinguish having a Nigerian *parent* (s. 25(1)(c)) from having only a Nigerian *grandparent* (s. 26(2)(b)) when born abroad.
questions.explanation: Under section 25(1)(c), anyone born outside Nigeria with at least one Nigerian citizen parent is automatically a Nigerian citizen by birth. (By contrast, if born abroad with only a Nigerian grandparent, they register at full age under s. 26(2)(b).)
questions.trap: Students often confuse 'grandparent' (which triggers s. 26 registration when born abroad) with 'parent' (which grants s. 25 birth citizenship).
questions.mnemonic: Born abroad with Nigerian parent = birth citizen; grandparent only = registration.

askPresets.answer: Under section 25(1)(c), anyone born outside Nigeria with at least one Nigerian citizen parent is automatically a Nigerian citizen by birth. (By contrast, if born abroad with only a Nigerian grandparent, they register at full age under s. 26(2)(b).)
Registration under s. 26(2)(b) applies when a *grandparent* (not a parent) is a citizen for a child born abroad.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Under section 26(2) of the 1999 Constitution, which two categories of persons may apply to the President for citizenship by registration?

options.text: Any foreign investor who employs 50 Nigerian citizens
options.why: Employment creation is not a ground for citizenship by registration under section 26.
options.whyWrong: Employment creation is not a ground for citizenship by registration under section 26.

options.text: Any foreign man or woman married to a Nigerian citizen for one year
options.why: Section 26(2)(a) specifies 'any woman' married to a Nigerian citizen; foreign husbands apply under section 27 naturalisation.
options.whyWrong: Section 26(2)(a) specifies 'any woman' married to a Nigerian citizen; foreign husbands apply under section 27 naturalisation.

options.text: Any foreigner who has lived in Nigeria for 15 continuous years
options.why: 15 years residence leads to naturalisation under section 27, not registration under section 26.
options.whyWrong: 15 years residence leads to naturalisation under section 27, not registration under section 26.

options.text: Any foreign woman married (or formerly married) to a Nigerian citizen, and any adult born abroad with a Nigerian grandparent
options.why: Section 26(2)(a)–(b) specifies any woman who is or has been married to a Nigerian citizen, and every person of full age and capacity born outside Nigeria any of whose grandparents is a Nigerian citizen.

questions.hint: Check the exact wording of section 26(2)(a) and (b) in the 1999 Constitution.
questions.explanation: Section 26(2) restricts citizenship by registration to (a) any woman who is or has been married to a citizen of Nigeria, and (b) any person of full age and capacity born outside Nigeria any of whose grandparents is a Nigerian citizen (subject to good character, domicile intent, and Oath of Allegiance).
questions.trap: Because gender equality feels intuitive, candidates frequently pick 'any foreign man or woman married to a Nigerian', missing the literal wording of section 26(2)(a).
questions.mnemonic: Registration under s. 26: woman married to a Nigerian, or adult born abroad with a Nigerian grandparent.

askPresets.answer: Section 26(2) restricts citizenship by registration to (a) any woman who is or has been married to a citizen of Nigeria, and (b) any person of full age and capacity born outside Nigeria any of whose grandparents is a Nigerian citizen (subject to good character, domicile intent, and Oath of Allegiance).
Section 26(2)(a) specifies 'any woman' married to a Nigerian citizen; foreign husbands apply under section 27 naturalisation.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Besides 15 years residence, good character, and taking the Oath of Allegiance, what local requirement must an applicant for naturalisation satisfy under section 27(2)(d)?

options.text: Approval by a two-thirds vote of the National Assembly
options.why: Naturalisation is granted by the President upon statutory conditions, not by parliamentary vote.
options.whyWrong: Naturalisation is granted by the President upon statutory conditions, not by parliamentary vote.

options.text: Sponsorship by two registered political parties
options.why: Political party sponsorship applies to elections, never to naturalisation.
options.whyWrong: Political party sponsorship applies to elections, never to naturalisation.

options.text: Opinion of the State Governor that the applicant is acceptable to the local community and assimilated into its way of life
options.why: Section 27(2)(d) requires the Governor of the proposed State of residence to certify that the applicant is acceptable to the local community and has assimilated into Nigerians' way of life there.

options.text: Ownership of at least ten hectares of farmland
options.why: Property ownership is not required by section 27(2).
options.whyWrong: Property ownership is not required by section 27(2).

questions.hint: Ask which State chief executive checks whether the newcomer fits peacefully into the local community.
questions.explanation: Under section 27(2)(d), a naturalisation applicant must satisfy the President that, in the opinion of the Governor of the State of residence, they are acceptable to the local community and assimilated into the local way of life.
questions.trap: Students know the 15-year rule yet often miss the State Governor's local-acceptance and assimilation requirement.
questions.mnemonic: Naturalisation needs 15 years plus the State Governor's local-acceptance nod.

askPresets.answer: Under section 27(2)(d), a naturalisation applicant must satisfy the President that, in the opinion of the Governor of the State of residence, they are acceptable to the local community and assimilated into the local way of life.
Naturalisation is granted by the President upon statutory conditions, not by parliamentary vote.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: A foreign national becomes a Nigerian citizen by naturalisation under section 27, while already holding a passport from another country where they were NOT a citizen by birth. Under section 28(2), what must happen?

options.text: They may keep both passports indefinitely without restriction
options.why: Only citizens of Nigeria by birth (or those holding birth citizenship of another country) avoid the renunciation condition in s. 28.
options.whyWrong: Only citizens of Nigeria by birth (or those holding birth citizenship of another country) avoid the renunciation condition in s. 28.

options.text: They forfeit the right to own property in Nigeria
options.why: Property rights under s. 43 belong to all Nigerian citizens.
options.whyWrong: Property rights under s. 43 belong to all Nigerian citizens.

options.text: They must renounce Nigerian citizenship immediately
options.why: They must renounce the prior *non-birth foreign* citizenship within 12 months to keep Nigerian citizenship.
options.whyWrong: They must renounce the prior *non-birth foreign* citizenship within 12 months to keep Nigerian citizenship.

options.text: The grant is conditional upon effectively renouncing the other non-birth citizenship within 12 months
options.why: Section 28(2) makes registration or naturalisation conditional upon renouncing non-birth citizenship of any other country within 12 months.

questions.hint: Compare birth citizens with registered/naturalised citizens under section 28(1)–(2).
questions.explanation: Section 28(1)–(2) allows Nigerian citizens by birth to retain dual citizenship, while requiring registered or naturalised citizens to renounce any non-birth foreign citizenship within 12 months (or forfeit Nigerian citizenship).
questions.trap: Knowing Nigeria permits dual citizenship for birth citizens, many students wrongly assume naturalised citizens have the exact same unrestricted rule.
questions.mnemonic: Birth citizens keep dual passports; naturalised must drop non-birth passports in 12 months.

askPresets.answer: Section 28(1)–(2) allows Nigerian citizens by birth to retain dual citizenship, while requiring registered or naturalised citizens to renounce any non-birth foreign citizenship within 12 months (or forfeit Nigerian citizenship).
Only citizens of Nigeria by birth (or those holding birth citizenship of another country) avoid the renunciation condition in s. 28.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Under section 29(3) of the 1999 Constitution, when may the President withhold registration of a Nigerian citizen's declaration of renunciation of citizenship?

options.text: If the declaration is made during any war in which Nigeria is physically involved, or if the President believes it is otherwise contrary to public policy
options.why: Section 29(3)(a)–(b) allows the President to withhold registration during physical war involving Nigeria or where contrary to public policy.

options.text: Whenever the citizen owes local government property rates
options.why: Unpaid property rates are civil/tax enforcement matters, not grounds under s. 29(3).
options.whyWrong: Unpaid property rates are civil/tax enforcement matters, not grounds under s. 29(3).

options.text: Whenever the citizen belongs to an opposition political party
options.why: Political opinion cannot be used to block renunciation or discriminate under s. 42.
options.whyWrong: Political opinion cannot be used to block renunciation or discriminate under s. 42.

options.text: Only if the citizen has not turned 35 years old
options.why: Under s. 29(1) and (4), 'full age' is 18 years (or married woman), not 35.
options.whyWrong: Under s. 29(1) and (4), 'full age' is 18 years (or married woman), not 35.

questions.hint: Think about national security emergencies where a state restricts citizens from dropping nationality.
questions.explanation: Under section 29(1)–(3), any Nigerian citizen of full age (18 or married) may declare renunciation, and the President registers it unless made during a war physically involving Nigeria or deemed contrary to public policy.
questions.trap: Candidates sometimes confuse presidential candidate age (35) with 'full age' for renunciation (18).
questions.mnemonic: Renunciation can be held back during war or for public policy.

askPresets.answer: Under section 29(1)–(3), any Nigerian citizen of full age (18 or married) may declare renunciation, and the President registers it unless made during a war physically involving Nigeria or deemed contrary to public policy.
Under s. 29(1) and (4), 'full age' is 18 years (or married woman), not 35.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Which Nigerian citizen CANNOT be deprived of citizenship by the President under section 30 of the 1999 Constitution?

options.text: A citizen by naturalisation jailed for 5 years within 4 years of naturalising
options.why: Section 30(1) expressly allows depriving a naturalised citizen sentenced to at least 3 years within 7 years of naturalisation.
options.whyWrong: Section 30(1) expressly allows depriving a naturalised citizen sentenced to at least 3 years within 7 years of naturalisation.

options.text: A citizen by birth
options.why: Both subsections (1) and (2) of section 30 expressly exclude any citizen of Nigeria by birth from deprivation.

options.text: A citizen by registration proved disloyal toward Nigeria
options.why: Section 30(2)(a) requires the President to deprive non-birth citizens (registration or naturalisation) proved disloyal.
options.whyWrong: Section 30(2)(a) requires the President to deprive non-birth citizens (registration or naturalisation) proved disloyal.

options.text: A citizen by naturalisation who unlawfully trades with an enemy during war
options.why: Section 30(2)(b) mandates deprivation of non-birth citizens who unlawfully trade with the enemy in wartime.
options.whyWrong: Section 30(2)(b) mandates deprivation of non-birth citizens who unlawfully trade with the enemy in wartime.

questions.hint: Check which category of citizenship enjoys absolute constitutional protection against deprivation.
questions.explanation: Section 30 empowers the President to deprive naturalised or registered citizens of citizenship for serious post-naturalisation imprisonment (s. 30(1)) or disloyalty/trading with an enemy (s. 30(2)), while strictly protecting every citizen by birth.
questions.trap: Students sometimes think severe treason strips a citizen by birth of citizenship, whereas s. 30 protects birth citizens completely (punishment is via criminal law, not denationalisation).
questions.mnemonic: Citizens by birth can never be stripped of citizenship.

askPresets.answer: Section 30 empowers the President to deprive naturalised or registered citizens of citizenship for serious post-naturalisation imprisonment (s. 30(1)) or disloyalty/trading with an enemy (s. 30(2)), while strictly protecting every citizen by birth.
Section 30(2)(a) requires the President to deprive non-birth citizens (registration or naturalisation) proved disloyal.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Under sections 131(a) and 177(a) of the 1999 Constitution, which category of Nigerian citizens is qualified to be elected President or State Governor?

options.text: Any citizen by birth, registration, or naturalisation
options.why: Sections 131(a) and 177(a) specifically require citizenship of Nigeria *by birth*.
options.whyWrong: Sections 131(a) and 177(a) specifically require citizenship of Nigeria *by birth*.

options.text: Citizens of Nigeria by birth only
options.why: Both s. 131(a) (President) and s. 177(a) (Governor) require the candidate to be a citizen of Nigeria by birth.

options.text: Any citizen by naturalisation who has lived in Nigeria for 20 years
options.why: Even 20 years residence does not satisfy the birth-citizenship requirement for President or Governor.
options.whyWrong: Even 20 years residence does not satisfy the birth-citizenship requirement for President or Governor.

options.text: Only citizens by registration who speak three Nigerian languages
options.why: Language ability is not a constitutional qualification, and registration does not suffice for President or Governor.
options.whyWrong: Language ability is not a constitutional qualification, and registration does not suffice for President or Governor.

questions.hint: Notice the extra word added in sections 131(a) and 177(a) compared with section 65.
questions.explanation: Whereas section 65(1) requires legislative candidates to be 'a citizen of Nigeria', sections 131(a) and 177(a) explicitly require a candidate for President or State Governor to be 'a citizen of Nigeria by birth'.
questions.trap: Because naturalised citizens enjoy most civil rights, students often assume they can also run for Governor or President.
questions.mnemonic: President and Governor must be citizens by birth.

askPresets.answer: Whereas section 65(1) requires legislative candidates to be 'a citizen of Nigeria', sections 131(a) and 177(a) explicitly require a candidate for President or State Governor to be 'a citizen of Nigeria by birth'.
Sections 131(a) and 177(a) specifically require citizenship of Nigeria *by birth*.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Which of the following is an explicit constitutional duty of every Nigerian citizen under section 24 of the 1999 Constitution?

options.text: Declare income honestly to appropriate and lawful agencies and pay tax promptly
options.why: Section 24(f) obliges every citizen to declare income honestly and pay tax promptly.

options.text: Join a registered political party before age 25
options.why: Joining a political party is voluntary under s. 40, never a duty.
options.whyWrong: Joining a political party is voluntary under s. 40, never a duty.

options.text: Serve at least one term in a Local Government Council
options.why: Standing for election is a voluntary civic right, not a duty under s. 24.
options.whyWrong: Standing for election is a voluntary civic right, not a duty under s. 24.

options.text: Attend weekly town-hall meetings in Abuja
options.why: No such attendance requirement exists in section 24.
options.whyWrong: No such attendance requirement exists in section 24.

questions.hint: Recall the six duties listed in section 24(a)–(f), ending with tax honesty.
questions.explanation: Section 24 requires every citizen to abide by the Constitution, respect national symbols and legitimate authorities, defend Nigeria, respect other citizens' dignity, contribute positively to their community, assist lawful agencies in keeping order, and declare income honestly and pay tax promptly.
questions.trap: Distractors mix voluntary political participation (like joining parties) with mandatory civic duties (like honest tax payment).
questions.mnemonic: Section 24 duties include obeying laws, defending Nigeria, and paying taxes promptly.

askPresets.answer: Section 24 requires every citizen to abide by the Constitution, respect national symbols and legitimate authorities, defend Nigeria, respect other citizens' dignity, contribute positively to their community, assist lawful agencies in keeping order, and declare income honestly and pay tax promptly.
Joining a political party is voluntary under s. 40, never a duty.

questions.stem: Section 14(2)(b) of the 1999 Constitution declares that the primary purpose of government shall be

options.text: preserving the monopoly of a single ruling party
options.why: Nigeria is a multi-party democracy; s. 14(1) bases the state on democracy and social justice.
options.whyWrong: Nigeria is a multi-party democracy; s. 14(1) bases the state on democracy and social justice.

options.text: the security and welfare of the people
options.why: Section 14(2)(b) states verbatim that 'the security and welfare of the people shall be the primary purpose of government'.

options.text: maximising customs duties above all social services
options.why: Revenue collection funds governance, while security and welfare of the people are the primary purpose.

options.text: concentrating all administrative powers in Abuja
options.why: Nigeria is a federation with States and elected local councils, not total centralisation.
options.whyWrong: Nigeria is a federation with States and elected local councils, not total centralisation.

questions.explanation: Alongside declaring that sovereignty belongs to the people (s. 14(2)(a)), section 14(2)(b) establishes that the security and welfare of the people shall be the primary purpose of government.
questions.trap: This core phrase appears directly in the text of section 14(2)(b) and anchors the state-obligations topic in the syllabus.

questions.stem: A foreign doctor has lived in Nigeria continuously for the past 12 months, and also lived in Nigeria for various periods totalling 14 years earlier in the last 20 years (15 years total). Under section 27(2)(g), does this satisfy the residency rule for naturalisation?

options.text: No, because all 15 years must be strictly unbroken with zero trips abroad
options.why: Section 27(2)(g)(ii) explicitly provides an alternative aggregate path alongside the 15-continuous-year rule.
options.whyWrong: Section 27(2)(g)(ii) explicitly provides an alternative aggregate path alongside the 15-continuous-year rule.

options.text: Yes, because doctors automatically skip all residency rules
options.why: Professional qualification helps meet useful-contribution criteria (s. 27(2)(e)), not waiving residency.
options.whyWrong: Professional qualification helps meet useful-contribution criteria (s. 27(2)(e)), not waiving residency.

options.text: No, because 25 years aggregate residence is required
options.why: The Constitution requires 15 years aggregate out of 20 years, not 25.
options.whyWrong: The Constitution requires 15 years aggregate out of 20 years, not 25.

options.text: Yes, because s. 27(2)(g)(ii) accepts 12 continuous months immediately before applying plus at least 15 years aggregate within the preceding 20 years
options.why: Section 27(2)(g)(ii) permits naturalisation after 12 continuous months immediately preceding application combined with an aggregate of at least 15 years in the preceding 20 years.

questions.stem: Under sections 77(2) and 117(2) of the 1999 Constitution, at what minimum age is a Nigerian citizen residing in Nigeria entitled to register as a voter?

options.text: 18 years

options.text: 16 years
options.why: 16 is below Nigeria's constitutional voting age.
options.whyWrong: 16 is below Nigeria's constitutional voting age.

options.text: 21 years

options.whyWrong: 21 was the historical age before universal 18+ adult suffrage in modern Nigerian constitutions.

options.text: 25 years
options.why: 25 is the minimum age to contest for the House of Representatives or a State House of Assembly, not to vote.
options.whyWrong: 25 is the minimum age to contest for the House of Representatives or a State House of Assembly, not to vote.

questions.hint: Distinguish the age to cast a ballot from the age to run for Parliament.
questions.explanation: Sections 77(2) and 117(2) — extended to Presidential, Governorship, and Local Council elections by ss. 132(5), 178(5), and 7(4) — entitle every Nigerian citizen aged 18 years and above residing in Nigeria at registration to register as a voter.

options.why: These were the old pre-2017 age limits before the Fourth Alteration (No. 27) Act lowered House of Reps and President.
options.whyWrong: These were the old pre-2017 age limits before the Fourth Alteration (No. 27) Act lowered House of Reps and President.

options.text: 25, 30 and 35 years
options.why: Senate minimum age remained 35 years under section 65(1)(a), rather than dropping to 30.
options.whyWrong: Senate minimum age remained 35 years under section 65(1)(a), rather than dropping to 30.

options.text: 25, 35 and 35 years

options.text: 18, 25 and 30 years

options.whyWrong: 18 is the minimum voting age, not a legislative candidacy age.

questions.stem: Under sections 66(1)(f) and 137(1)(g) of the 1999 Constitution, a person employed in the public service of the Federation or of a State who seeks election must resign, withdraw, or retire at least how many days before the election?

options.text: 7 days before the election
options.why: 7 days is far shorter than the constitutional notice period.
options.whyWrong: 7 days is far shorter than the constitutional notice period.

options.text: 90 days before the election
options.why: 90 days is the recall referendum window (s. 69(b)), not public-service resignation.
options.whyWrong: 90 days is the recall referendum window (s. 69(b)), not public-service resignation.

options.text: 30 days before the date of election
options.why: Sections 66(1)(f) and 137(1)(g) disqualify any public servant who has not resigned, withdrawn, or retired at least 30 days before the election date.

options.text: 180 days before the election
options.why: 180 days is the election tribunal judgment window (s. 285(6)).
options.whyWrong: 180 days is the election tribunal judgment window (s. 285(6)).

questions.hint: Think of one month before polling day.
questions.explanation: To prevent civil servants from using official machinery in campaigns, sections 66(1)(f), 107(1)(f), 137(1)(g), and 182(1)(g) require resignation, withdrawal, or retirement from public service at least 30 days before the election.
questions.trap: Students often confuse the 30-day resignation clock with 90-day recall or 60-day ministerial nomination deadlines.
questions.mnemonic: Civil servants step down at least 30 days before polling day.

questions.subject: government
questions.topic: The electoral process and presidential elections
questions.stem: In a presidential election with three candidates under section 134(2), a candidate is duly elected only by winning the highest number of votes cast AND scoring not less than

options.text: \frac{1}{4} (25%) of the votes cast in each of at least \frac{2}{3} of all the States in the Federation and the FCT
options.why: Section 134(2)(b) requires at least one-quarter of the votes cast in each of at least two-thirds of all States and the FCT.

options.text: an absolute majority of votes in Lagos, Kano, and Rivers alone
options.why: Winning large totals in a few States without broad national spread fails section 134(2)(b).
options.whyWrong: Winning large totals in a few States without broad national spread fails section 134(2)(b).

options.text: \frac{1}{2} (50%) of the votes cast in every single one of the 36 States
options.why: 50% in every State is far higher than the constitutional one-quarter in two-thirds threshold.
options.whyWrong: 50% in every State is far higher than the constitutional one-quarter in two-thirds threshold.

options.text: a simple majority in just \frac{1}{3} of the States
options.why: One-third of States is too narrow; section 134 requires one-quarter in at least two-thirds of States and the FCT.
options.whyWrong: One-third of States is too narrow; section 134 requires one-quarter in at least two-thirds of States and the FCT.

questions.hint: Pair the 25% floor per state with the two-thirds national geographic spread.
questions.explanation: Section 134(2) prevents purely sectional presidential victories by requiring both the highest national vote total and at least one-quarter (25%) of votes cast in each of at least two-thirds of all States and the Federal Capital Territory, Abuja.
questions.trap: Candidates occasionally misremember the fraction as one-third of states or 50% in two-thirds of states.
questions.mnemonic: Presidential formula: highest votes + 25% in two-thirds of States and FCT.

askPresets.answer: Section 134(2) prevents purely sectional presidential victories by requiring both the highest national vote total and at least one-quarter (25%) of votes cast in each of at least two-thirds of all States and the Federal Capital Territory, Abuja.
50% in every State is far higher than the constitutional one-quarter in two-thirds threshold.

questions.subject: government
questions.topic: The electoral process and presidential elections
questions.stem: If three or more candidates contest a Presidential election and NO candidate meets the section 134(2) spread requirement, which two candidates advance to the second election under section 134(3)?

options.text: All candidates who scored at least 10% nationwide
options.why: Only two candidates contest the second election under section 134(3)–(4).
options.whyWrong: Only two candidates contest the second election under section 134(3)–(4).

options.text: The top two candidates by total nationwide votes regardless of State majorities
options.why: Section 134(3)(b) specifically checks majority of votes in the highest number of States, not automatically second-place total votes.
options.whyWrong: Section 134(3)(b) specifically checks majority of votes in the highest number of States, not automatically second-place total votes.

options.text: The oldest and youngest candidates on the ballot
options.why: Age plays no part in selecting run-off candidates.
options.whyWrong: Age plays no part in selecting run-off candidates.

options.text: The candidate with highest total votes, and the candidate with the majority of votes in the highest number of States
options.why: Section 134(3)(a)–(b) pairs the highest overall vote-scorer with the remaining candidate who won a majority of votes in the highest number of States (breaking ties by highest total votes).

questions.hint: Look closely at subsection (3)(b) — it rewards winning majorities across States, not just raw runner-up total!
questions.explanation: Under section 134(3), the presidential run-off (held within 21 days under s. 134(4)) pits (a) the highest overall vote-scorer against (b) the remaining candidate with a majority of votes in the highest number of States (using total votes only to break a tie in State majorities).
questions.trap: Nearly every student guesses 'top two by total votes', missing section 134(3)(b)'s State-majority rule.
questions.mnemonic: Run-off pairs top total votes vs top State-majority winner.

askPresets.answer: Under section 134(3), the presidential run-off (held within 21 days under s. 134(4)) pits (a) the highest overall vote-scorer against (b) the remaining candidate with a majority of votes in the highest number of States (using total votes only to break a tie in State majorities).
Section 134(3)(b) specifically checks majority of votes in the highest number of States, not automatically second-place total votes.
