questions.topic: The electoral process and governorship elections
questions.stem: Under section 179(2) of the 1999 Constitution, a governorship candidate in a multi-candidate race must score the highest votes AND at least \frac{1}{4} of all votes cast in each of at least

options.text: \frac{1}{2} of the Senatorial districts in the State
options.why: Governorship spread is measured by Local Government Areas, not Senatorial districts.
options.whyWrong: Governorship spread is measured by Local Government Areas, not Senatorial districts.

options.text: \frac{2}{3} of all the Local Government Areas in the State
options.why: Section 179(2)(b) applies the 25% spread rule across at least two-thirds of all Local Government Areas in the State.

options.text: \frac{3}{4} of the State constituencies
options.why: The fraction is two-thirds of LGAs, not three-quarters of State constituencies.
options.whyWrong: The fraction is two-thirds of LGAs, not three-quarters of State constituencies.

options.text: every ward in the State capital
options.why: A governor must show spread across LGAs in the State, not only the State capital.
options.whyWrong: A governor must show spread across LGAs in the State, not only the State capital.

questions.hint: Scale the presidential State-spread rule down to the sub-units inside a State.
questions.explanation: Just as the President needs 25% in two-thirds of States and FCT (s. 134), section 179(2)(b) requires a Governor to win highest votes plus at least one-quarter of votes in at least two-thirds of all Local Government Areas in the State.
questions.trap: Students sometimes swap LGAs for Senatorial districts or wards.
questions.mnemonic: Governor needs highest votes + 25% in two-thirds of the State's LGAs.

askPresets.answer: Just as the President needs 25% in two-thirds of States and FCT (s. 134), section 179(2)(b) requires a Governor to win highest votes plus at least one-quarter of votes in at least two-thirds of all Local Government Areas in the State.

questions.topic: The electoral process and electoral timing
questions.stem: Under section 132(2) of the 1999 Constitution (as altered), INEC must hold a general Presidential election within what window before the expiration of the incumbent term?

options.text: At any date selected by the outgoing President
options.why: Under s. 132(1), INEC appoints the election date in accordance with the Electoral Act, not the outgoing President.
options.whyWrong: Under s. 132(1), INEC appoints the election date in accordance with the Electoral Act, not the outgoing President.

options.text: Not earlier than 60 days and not later than 7 days before term expiration
options.why: The 60-to-30-day window belonged to the original unamended 1999 text before the 2010 Alterations widened it to 150–30 days.
options.whyWrong: The 60-to-30-day window belonged to the original unamended 1999 text before the 2010 Alterations widened it to 150–30 days.

options.text: Within 14 days after the term has expired
options.why: Elections occur before term expiration so transition happens smoothly, not after.
options.whyWrong: Elections occur before term expiration so transition happens smoothly, not after.

options.text: Not earlier than 150 days and not later than 30 days before term expiration
options.why: Section 132(2) (First and Second Alterations, 2010) requires the election to be held between 150 days and 30 days before the last holder's term expires.

questions.hint: Remember the 2010 First and Second Alterations widened the pre-expiration window to allow petition resolution.
questions.explanation: The First and Second Alterations (2010) amended section 132(2) (and ss. 76, 116, 178) so elections take place not earlier than 150 days and not later than 30 days before term expiration.
questions.trap: Older pre-2010 notes quote 60 to 30 days; the amended Constitution sets 150 to 30 days.
questions.mnemonic: Elections happen 150 to 30 days before the term ends.

questions.subject: government
questions.concept: Recall of National or State legislators
questions.stem: Under sections 69 and 110 of the 1999 Constitution, a legislator's constituents can complete a recall only if a petition verified by INEC is signed by more than \frac{1}{2} of registered constituency voters and then approved in a referendum within 90 days by

options.text: a two-thirds majority of all voters in the State
options.why: The recall referendum covers only the member's constituency and requires a simple majority, not a statewide two-thirds vote.
options.whyWrong: The recall referendum covers only the member's constituency and requires a simple majority, not a statewide two-thirds vote.

options.text: the Governor and Speaker of the State Assembly
options.why: Recall is decided directly by constituency voters, not executive or presiding officers.
options.whyWrong: Recall is decided directly by constituency voters, not executive or presiding officers.

options.text: a simple majority of the votes of persons registered to vote in that member's constituency
options.why: Sections 69(b) and 110(b) require approval by a simple majority of registered voters in that member's constituency in an INEC referendum within 90 days.

options.text: a joint sitting of the National Judicial Council
options.why: The NJC handles judicial appointments and discipline, never legislative recall.
options.whyWrong: The NJC handles judicial appointments and discipline, never legislative recall.

questions.hint: Check both the referendum majority and who gets to vote in it.
questions.explanation: Under sections 69 and 110, recall takes two steps: (1) a petition signed by more than one-half of registered voters in the constituency verified by INEC, and (2) approval by a simple majority of registered constituency voters in an INEC referendum within 90 days.
questions.trap: Because the petition needs over half of registered voters, students often assume the referendum also requires a two-thirds supermajority.
questions.mnemonic: Recall = over half sign petition + simple majority in 90-day constituency vote.

questions.stem: Under Third Schedule Part I Item F paragraph 14 of the 1999 Constitution, what is the composition and minimum age requirement for INEC's national leadership?

options.text: A Chairman (≥ 30 years) and 7 National Commissioners
options.why: The minimum ages are 40 (Chairman) and 35 (National Commissioners and RECs), with 12 National Commissioners.
options.whyWrong: The minimum ages are 40 (Chairman) and 35 (National Commissioners and RECs), with 12 National Commissioners.

options.why: INEC has 12 National Commissioners (not 36), appointed by the President with Council of State consultation and Senate confirmation (s. 154).
options.whyWrong: INEC has 12 National Commissioners (not 36), appointed by the President with Council of State consultation and Senate confirmation (s. 154).

options.whyWrong: INEC members must be non-partisan and of unquestionable integrity, never party appointees.

options.why: Paragraph 14(1)–(3) specifies a Chairman (at least 40 years), 12 National Electoral Commissioners (at least 35 years), and one REC (at least 35 years) for each State and the FCT.

questions.stem: In appointing the Chairman and members of INEC under section 154(1) and (3), the President must

questions.stem: A candidate challenges the declared result of a Presidential election. Under section 239(1) of the 1999 Constitution, which court exercises exclusive original jurisdiction to hear the petition first?

options.text: The Federal High Court, Abuja
options.why: The Federal High Court has no original jurisdiction over Presidential election petitions.
options.whyWrong: The Federal High Court has no original jurisdiction over Presidential election petitions.

options.text: The Supreme Court of Nigeria
options.why: Under s. 233(2)(e), the Supreme Court hears *appeals* from the Court of Appeal in presidential election matters, not at first instance.
options.whyWrong: Under s. 233(2)(e), the Supreme Court hears *appeals* from the Court of Appeal in presidential election matters, not at first instance.

options.text: The Court of Appeal
options.why: Section 239(1) vests exclusive original jurisdiction over Presidential and Vice-Presidential election petitions in the Court of Appeal (duly constituted by at least three Justices).

options.text: The National and State Houses of Assembly Election Tribunal
options.why: Section 285(1) tribunals hear National and State Assembly petitions only.
options.whyWrong: Section 285(1) tribunals hear National and State Assembly petitions only.

questions.hint: Separate the court of first instance (s. 239) from the final appellate court (s. 233).
questions.explanation: Section 239(1)–(2) gives the Court of Appeal (with at least three Justices) exclusive original jurisdiction over Presidential election petitions; appeals then go as of right to the Supreme Court under section 233(2)(e).
questions.trap: Many students assume the highest election dispute starts directly at the Supreme Court, overlooking section 239(1).
questions.mnemonic: Presidential petitions start at Appeal, end at Supreme.

questions.concept: Election petition filing and judgment deadlines
questions.stem: Under section 285(5)–(7) of the 1999 Constitution (Second Alteration, 2010), what are the strict time limits to file an election petition, deliver tribunal judgment, and dispose of an appeal?

options.text: 60 days to file, 120 days for tribunal judgment, and 180 days for appeal
options.why: 60 days is for appeal disposal, not filing; 180 days is for tribunal judgment, not appeals.
options.whyWrong: 60 days is for appeal disposal, not filing; 180 days is for tribunal judgment, not appeals.

options.text: 30 days to file, 365 days for tribunal judgment, and 90 days for appeal
options.why: These longer windows do not match the constitutional deadlines in section 285(5)–(7).
options.whyWrong: These longer windows do not match the constitutional deadlines in section 285(5)–(7).

options.text: 14 days to file, 90 days for tribunal judgment, and 30 days for appeal
options.why: These numbers understate the constitutional timelines in section 285(5)–(7).
options.whyWrong: These numbers understate the constitutional timelines in section 285(5)–(7).

options.text: 21 days to file, 180 days for tribunal judgment, and 60 days for each appeal
options.why: Section 285(5)–(7) sets exactly 21 days from result declaration to file, 180 days from filing for judgment, and 60 days from judgment delivery to dispose of an appeal.

questions.hint: Order the three clocks from filing (shortest) to tribunal trial (longest) to appeal.
questions.explanation: Introduced by the Second Alteration Act 2010 to stop petitions from dragging across an entire four-year term, s. 285(5)–(7) sets 21 days to file, 180 days for the tribunal judgment, and 60 days to dispose of each appeal.
questions.trap: Mixing up the 21, 180, and 60 sequence is the classic trap on section 285.
questions.mnemonic: 21 to file, 180 to try, 60 to appeal.

options.text: By indirect election through State Governors
options.why: Both Federal and State legislative houses are filled by direct popular election (ss. 77(1), 117(1)).
options.whyWrong: Both Federal and State legislative houses are filled by direct popular election (ss. 77(1), 117(1)).

options.whyWrong: Section 49 explicitly prohibits any Federal constituency from falling within more than one State.

questions.topic: Political parties and freedom of association
questions.concept: Constitutional right to form parties and unions
questions.stem: Which section of the 1999 Constitution protects every person's right to form or belong to any political party, trade union, or other association for the protection of their interests?

options.text: Section 39 (freedom of expression)
options.why: Section 39 covers speech and the press rather than association.
options.whyWrong: Section 39 covers speech and the press rather than association.

options.text: Section 40 (right to peaceful assembly and association)
options.why: Section 40 specifically guarantees freedom to assemble freely and associate, naming political parties, trade unions, and interest associations.

options.text: Section 41 (freedom of movement)
options.why: Section 41 covers movement and residence throughout Nigeria.
options.whyWrong: Section 41 covers movement and residence throughout Nigeria.

options.whyWrong: Section 44 protects property rights against uncompensated compulsory acquisition.

questions.explanation: Section 40 protects peaceful assembly and association — explicitly naming political parties, trade unions, and other associations for protecting interests (subject to INEC's powers over unrecognised political parties).

questions.stem: A chamber of commerce wants to promote its preferred candidate in a Governorship election by raising campaign donations and canvassing for votes. Under section 221 of the 1999 Constitution, why is this prohibited?

options.text: Because governorship candidates spend only personal savings
options.why: Political parties may fund and sponsor candidates under the Constitution and Electoral Act.
options.whyWrong: Political parties may fund and sponsor candidates under the Constitution and Electoral Act.

options.text: Because citizens have no freedom of expression during election years

options.whyWrong: Citizens retain s. 39 expression rights, while s. 221 specifically bars non-party associations from vote canvassing and campaign funding.

options.text: Because trade and business groups cannot send petitions to lawmakers

options.whyWrong: Petitioning lawmakers is lawful pressure-group activity; s. 221 targets vote-canvassing and campaign contributions.

options.text: Because only a registered political party may canvass for votes or contribute to party funds or candidate election expenses
options.why: Section 221 forbids any association other than a political party from canvassing for votes or contributing to party funds or candidate election expenses.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Under section 222 of the 1999 Constitution, an association cannot function as a political party in Nigeria unless

options.text: its name and emblem highlight the dominant language of its founder's State
options.why: Section 222(e) strictly prohibits ethnic, religious, or geographically confined names, symbols, or logos.
options.whyWrong: Section 222(e) strictly prohibits ethnic, religious, or geographically confined names, symbols, or logos.

options.text: it establishes regional headquarters in at least three State capitals instead of Abuja
options.why: Section 222(f) requires the party headquarters to be situated specifically in the Federal Capital Territory, Abuja.
options.whyWrong: Section 222(f) requires the party headquarters to be situated specifically in the Federal Capital Territory, Abuja.

options.text: membership is open to every citizen, its name and logo carry no ethnic or religious connotation, and its headquarters is in Abuja
options.why: Section 222(b), (e), and (f) require open membership regardless of origin/sex/religion/ethnicity, no ethnic/religious/regional name or logo, and headquarters in FCT Abuja.

options.whyWrong: Section 222(c)–(d) requires registering a copy of the party constitution with INEC (and any alterations within 30 days).

questions.hint: Think about the constitutional safeguards designed to prevent sectional or regional parties.
questions.explanation: Section 222 sets six mandatory registration rules: registering national officers and constitution with INEC (alterations within 30 days), open citizenship membership, non-ethnic/non-religious/national names and logos, and headquarters in the FCT, Abuja.

questions.mnemonic: Open to all, national symbol, registered at INEC, HQ in Abuja.

questions.concept: Four-year party elections and two-thirds executive
questions.stem: Under section 223(1)–(2) of the 1999 Constitution, the executive committee or governing body of a political party must

options.text: draw its members exclusively from the six geopolitical zone capitals
options.why: Section 223(2)(b) measures spread by at least two-thirds of all States and the FCT.
options.whyWrong: Section 223(2)(b) measures spread by at least two-thirds of all States and the FCT.

options.text: appoint life-long party officers without periodic elections
options.why: Life-long appointments violate s. 223(1)(a) and (2)(a)'s 4-year democratic election rule.
options.whyWrong: Life-long appointments violate s. 223(1)(a) and (2)(a)'s 4-year democratic election rule.

options.text: be elected democratically at intervals not exceeding 4 years and include members from at least \frac{2}{3} of all States and the FCT
options.why: Section 223(2)(a)–(b) mandates democratic officer elections at least every 4 years and Federal Character across not less than two-thirds of all States and the FCT.

options.text: hold executive elections once every 8 years
options.why: The maximum interval under s. 223(2)(a) is 4 years, not 8 years.
options.whyWrong: The maximum interval under s. 223(2)(a) is 4 years, not 8 years.

questions.hint: Pair the 4-year democratic term with the two-thirds national spread rule.
questions.explanation: Section 223 enforces internal party democracy and national integration: principal officers and executive members must be democratically elected at regular intervals not exceeding 4 years, and must belong to different States numbering at least two-thirds of all States and the FCT.

questions.mnemonic: Party leaders face elections every 4 years and span two-thirds of States + FCT.

questions.stem: Under section 225(3)–(4) of the 1999 Constitution, if funds or assets are remitted to a Nigerian political party from outside Nigeria, the party must

options.text: convert them into naira within 90 days for party salaries
options.why: Foreign funds cannot be converted for party use; they must be surrendered to INEC within 21 days.
options.whyWrong: Foreign funds cannot be converted for party use; they must be surrendered to INEC within 21 days.

options.text: spend them only on printing voter education leaflets
options.why: A party cannot retain or spend foreign-remitted funds for any purpose.
options.whyWrong: A party cannot retain or spend foreign-remitted funds for any purpose.

options.text: pay or transfer them over to INEC within 21 days of receipt with required details
options.why: Section 225(3)–(4) forbids holding or retaining foreign funds/assets and requires transferring any foreign remittance to INEC within 21 days.

options.text: declare them only at the end of the four-year election cycle
options.why: Waiting until the end of an election cycle violates the 21-day handover duty in s. 225(4).
options.whyWrong: Waiting until the end of an election cycle violates the 21-day handover duty in s. 225(4).

questions.hint: Look at the strict constitutional barrier against foreign influence over Nigerian parties.
questions.explanation: Section 225(3) bars any political party from holding assets outside Nigeria or retaining funds remitted from abroad; section 225(4) requires handing any foreign remittance over to INEC within 21 days of receipt.
questions.trap: Students sometimes guess parties can keep foreign donations if declared or used for civic education, which s. 225(3)–(4) prohibits.
questions.mnemonic: Foreign party money goes straight to INEC within 21 days.

options.text: The National Assembly

options.whyWrong: Section 226(1) requires INEC to submit the annual party-accounts report to the National Assembly, not the President.

options.text: The Nigeria Police Council

options.whyWrong: The Police Council has no jurisdiction over party financial audits.

options.whyWrong: 50% of seats is far above the s. 225A threshold of even a single seat or ward.

questions.stem: Section 227 of the 1999 Constitution prohibits any person or association from organising, training, or equipping any group to use or display physical force or coercion for political objectives. This provision targets

questions.subject: government
questions.concept: Lawful pressure group methods vs party roles
questions.stem: Which activity is constitutionally lawful for a Nigerian teachers' union acting as a pressure group under sections 39, 40, and 221?

options.text: Sponsoring its union president on the ballot as a non-party independent candidate
options.why: Section 65(2)(b) and s. 221 allow only registered political parties to sponsor candidates.
options.whyWrong: Section 65(2)(b) and s. 221 allow only registered political parties to sponsor candidates.

options.text: Submitting public memoranda to a legislative committee and holding peaceful rallies for better school funding
options.why: Peaceful assembly (s. 40), expression (s. 39), and policy advocacy are lawful pressure-group methods, whereas s. 221 bars electoral funding/canvassing.

options.text: Donating union dues directly to a presidential candidate's campaign account
options.why: Section 221 prohibits non-party associations from contributing to candidate election expenses.
options.whyWrong: Section 221 prohibits non-party associations from contributing to candidate election expenses.

options.text: Organising an armed wing to block rival campaigns
options.why: Section 227 prohibits any association from organising coercive quasi-military groups.
options.whyWrong: Section 227 prohibits any association from organising coercive quasi-military groups.

questions.hint: Separate persuading lawmakers and public opinion (allowed) from sponsoring or funding elections (reserved for parties).
questions.explanation: Pressure groups such as trade unions form lawfully under section 40 and influence policy through petitions, lobbying, peaceful assembly, and public expression (ss. 39–40), while avoiding s. 221 vote-canvassing/campaign donations and s. 227 coercion.
questions.trap: Students sometimes forget that pressure groups CAN lobby and rally peacefully — they just cannot act as political parties under s. 221.
questions.mnemonic: Lobby and rally peacefully (ss. 39–40); never fund campaigns (s. 221).

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: If a registered Nigerian political party alters its party constitution, within how many days must it register the alteration at the principal office of INEC under section 222(d)?

options.text: Within 7 days
options.why: Section 222(d) grants 30 days, not 7 days.
options.whyWrong: Section 222(d) grants 30 days, not 7 days.

options.text: Within 180 days
options.why: 180 days is the election tribunal decision limit (s. 285(6)).
options.whyWrong: 180 days is the election tribunal decision limit (s. 285(6)).

options.text: Within 90 days
options.why: 90 days is the recall referendum window (s. 69(b)), not party constitution filing.
options.whyWrong: 90 days is the recall referendum window (s. 69(b)), not party constitution filing.

options.text: Within 30 days
options.why: Section 222(d) requires any alteration in a party's registered constitution to be registered at INEC's principal office within 30 days of making the alteration.

questions.hint: Remember the standard 1-month constitutional filing window in section 222(d).
questions.explanation: Under section 222(c)–(d), a party must keep its constitution registered at INEC's principal office and register any alteration within 30 days of making it.
questions.trap: 21 days (foreign funds, s. 225(4)) and 30 days (constitution alteration, s. 222(d)) sit side by side in Part III D — check which rule the stem asks for.
questions.mnemonic: Party rule changes go to INEC within 30 days; foreign funds within 21.

questions.stem: The proviso to section 40 of the 1999 Constitution states that freedom of association shall NOT derogate from

options.text: the power of State Governors to dissolve the National Assembly
options.why: State Governors have no power over the National Assembly.
options.whyWrong: State Governors have no power over the National Assembly.

options.text: the power of local chiefs to ban market unions
options.why: Section 40 protects forming trade unions and market associations.
options.whyWrong: Section 40 protects forming trade unions and market associations.

options.text: the power of the executive to outlaw opposition newspapers
options.why: Press freedom is protected by section 39.
options.whyWrong: Press freedom is protected by section 39.

options.text: the powers conferred on INEC with respect to political parties to which INEC does not accord recognition
options.why: The proviso to s. 40 expressly preserves INEC's constitutional powers regarding unrecognised political parties.

questions.hint: Recall why an unregistered political group cannot claim s. 40 forces INEC to put it on the ballot.
questions.explanation: Section 40's proviso clarifies that while everyone may associate freely, that right does not override INEC's constitutional authority under sections 222–225A to withhold or withdraw recognition from associations failing party registration or performance requirements.
questions.trap: Students often quote the first half of s. 40 without reading the INEC proviso at the end.
questions.mnemonic: Freedom to associate never forces INEC to register non-compliant parties.

questions.subject: government
questions.concept: Constitutional count of States and LGAs
questions.stem: Under section 3(1) and (6) of the 1999 Constitution, Nigeria consists of how many States, Local Government Areas, and Area Councils of the FCT?

options.text: 30 States, 589 LGAs, and 4 Area Councils
options.why: 30 States reflects the 1991 map before the 1996 creation of 6 more States.
options.whyWrong: 30 States reflects the 1991 map before the 1996 creation of 6 more States.

options.text: 36 States, 774 LGAs plus 6 extra Area Councils (780 total)
options.why: The 774 figure already equals 768 LGAs plus 6 FCT Area Councils.
options.whyWrong: The 774 figure already equals 768 LGAs plus 6 FCT Area Councils.

options.text: 36 States, 768 Local Government Areas, and 6 Area Councils of the FCT (774 local areas total)
options.why: Section 3(1) names 36 States, and s. 3(6) specifies 768 LGAs plus 6 Area Councils of the FCT (774 in First Schedule Parts I–II).

options.text: 19 States, 301 LGAs, and the Federal Capital Territory
options.why: 19 States reflects the 1976 structure under the 1979 Constitution, not the 1999 Constitution.
options.whyWrong: 19 States reflects the 1976 structure under the 1979 Constitution, not the 1999 Constitution.

questions.hint: Watch carefully how 768 and 6 add up to 774!
questions.explanation: Section 3(1) names Nigeria's 36 States, while section 3(6) specifies 768 Local Government Areas in Part I of the First Schedule and 6 Area Councils for the FCT in Part II — making 774 local council areas in total.
questions.trap: Adding 6 on top of 774 (to get 780) is a very common counting mistake; 774 already includes the 6 FCT Area Councils.
questions.mnemonic: 36 States + FCT; 768 LGAs + 6 FCT Area Councils = 774.

questions.subject: government
questions.topic: Federalism in Nigeria and legislative lists
questions.stem: Under section 4(2)–(3) and Part I of the Second Schedule to the 1999 Constitution, which group of subjects belongs strictly to the Exclusive Legislative List?

options.text: Defence, currency and legal tender, external affairs, and aviation
options.why: Items 3 (aviation), 15 (currency), 17 (defence), and 26 (external affairs) all sit on the Exclusive Legislative List for the National Assembly alone.

options.text: Markets, motor parks, and street naming
options.why: Markets, motor parks, and street naming belong to Local Government Councils under the Fourth Schedule.
options.whyWrong: Markets, motor parks, and street naming belong to Local Government Councils under the Fourth Schedule.

options.text: Collection of tenement rates and bicycle licences
options.why: Tenement rates and bicycle licences sit in the Fourth Schedule for Local Government Councils.
options.whyWrong: Tenement rates and bicycle licences sit in the Fourth Schedule for Local Government Councils.

options.text: Antiquities, archives, and university education shared with States
options.why: Antiquities, archives, and higher education appear on the Concurrent Legislative List (Part II of the Second Schedule).
options.whyWrong: Antiquities, archives, and higher education appear on the Concurrent Legislative List (Part II of the Second Schedule).

questions.hint: Look for national sovereign functions that only Abuja may legislate on.
questions.explanation: Part I of the Second Schedule lists 68 Exclusive items — including defence, currency, foreign affairs, aviation, citizenship, census, and police — on which only the National Assembly can legislate under s. 4(3).
questions.trap: Shared items like higher education or archives sit on the Concurrent List, tempting candidates away from purely Exclusive items.
questions.mnemonic: Exclusive List = army, naira, passports, census, planes, embassies.

askPresets.answer: Part I of the Second Schedule lists 68 Exclusive items — including defence, currency, foreign affairs, aviation, citizenship, census, and police — on which only the National Assembly can legislate under s. 4(3).
Antiquities, archives, and higher education appear on the Concurrent Legislative List (Part II of the Second Schedule).

questions.subject: government
questions.topic: Federalism in Nigeria and legislative lists
questions.stem: If a subject is NOT included in either the Exclusive Legislative List or the Concurrent Legislative List of the 1999 Constitution, which legislature has power to make laws on it under section 4(7)(a)?

options.text: The House of Assembly of a State (residual powers)
options.why: Section 4(7)(a) grants State Houses of Assembly power over any matter not included in the Exclusive Legislative List (and outside federal Concurrent items).

options.text: The Senate alone
options.why: Unlisted residual matters belong to State Houses of Assembly, not the federal Senate.
options.whyWrong: Unlisted residual matters belong to State Houses of Assembly, not the federal Senate.

options.text: The Federal Executive Council
options.why: The Federal Executive Council is an executive body, not a legislature.
options.whyWrong: The Federal Executive Council is an executive body, not a legislature.

options.text: The Supreme Court
options.why: Courts interpret laws rather than enacting statutes.
options.whyWrong: Courts interpret laws rather than enacting statutes.

questions.hint: In a federation, who keeps the 'leftover' residual basket not assigned to the centre?
questions.explanation: Under section 4(7)(a), residual legislative powers — matters excluded from the Exclusive List and not assigned to the federal legislature — belong to the Houses of Assembly of the States.
questions.trap: In some federations (like Canada) residual power sits at the centre, so students sometimes pick the federal legislature; in Nigeria (and the USA), residual power sits with the States.
questions.mnemonic: Unlisted = Residual = State Houses of Assembly.

askPresets.answer: Under section 4(7)(a), residual legislative powers — matters excluded from the Exclusive List and not assigned to the federal legislature — belong to the Houses of Assembly of the States.
Unlisted residual matters belong to State Houses of Assembly, not the federal Senate.

questions.subject: government
questions.topic: Federalism in Nigeria and legislative conflicts
questions.stem: When a Law enacted by a State House of Assembly on a Concurrent List matter conflicts with a law validly made by the National Assembly, section 4(5) declares that

options.text: the State Law prevails inside that State
options.why: Section 4(5) makes the valid National Assembly law prevail, not the State Law.
options.whyWrong: Section 4(5) makes the valid National Assembly law prevail, not the State Law.

options.text: the National Assembly law prevails, and the State Law is void to the extent of the inconsistency
options.why: Section 4(5) states verbatim that the National Assembly law prevails and the State Law is void to the extent of the inconsistency.

options.text: both laws are suspended until amended by a joint sitting
options.why: Only the inconsistent portion of the State Law becomes void; the valid Federal law operates immediately.
options.whyWrong: Only the inconsistent portion of the State Law becomes void; the valid Federal law operates immediately.

options.text: the State Governor decides which law applies
options.why: Constitutional priority under s. 4(5) is a rule of law, not Governor's choice.
options.whyWrong: Constitutional priority under s. 4(5) is a rule of law, not Governor's choice.

questions.hint: Recall the constitutional doctrine of covering the field / federal legislative supremacy in section 4(5).
questions.explanation: Section 4(5) resolves Concurrent List collisions: if any State Law is inconsistent with a valid National Assembly law, the federal law prevails and the State Law is void to the extent of the inconsistency.
questions.trap: Students sometimes think the *entire* State statute is struck down, whereas s. 4(5) voids it 'to the extent of the inconsistency'.
questions.mnemonic: Federal law wins Concurrent clashes; only the clashing State part is void.

askPresets.answer: Section 4(5) resolves Concurrent List collisions: if any State Law is inconsistent with a valid National Assembly law, the federal law prevails and the State Law is void to the extent of the inconsistency.
Only the inconsistent portion of the State Law becomes void; the valid Federal law operates immediately.

questions.subject: government
questions.topic: Federalism in Nigeria and state creation
questions.concept: Creating a new State under s. 8(1)
questions.stem: Creating a new State under section 8(1) of the 1999 Constitution requires several hurdles, including a \frac{2}{3} request from representatives of the area, approval by \frac{2}{3} of the area's people in a referendum, approval by a simple majority of all States, and finally

options.text: an executive proclamation signed solely by the President
options.why: State creation requires legislative and popular steps ending in National Assembly resolutions and an Act, never a solo proclamation.
options.whyWrong: State creation requires legislative and popular steps ending in National Assembly resolutions and an Act, never a solo proclamation.

options.text: a resolution passed by a \frac{2}{3} majority of members of each House of the National Assembly
options.why: Section 8(1)(d) requires the proposal to be approved by a resolution passed by two-thirds majority of members of each House of the National Assembly (followed by the enabling Act).

options.text: consent of the Supreme Court sitting in full panel
options.why: The Supreme Court does not approve proposals to create new States.
options.whyWrong: The Supreme Court does not approve proposals to create new States.

options.text: approval by the Commonwealth Secretariat
options.why: Internal State creation is purely a sovereign domestic constitutional process.
options.whyWrong: Internal State creation is purely a sovereign domestic constitutional process.

questions.hint: Remember how section 8(1) ends back at the National Assembly with a supermajority.
questions.explanation: Section 8(1) sets four tough stages to create a new State: (a) two-thirds request from NASS, State Assembly, and LGCs of the area; (b) two-thirds referendum approval in the area; (c) simple majority approval across all States of the Federation; and (d) two-thirds resolution of each House of the National Assembly.
questions.trap: Because military governments created States by decree before 1999, candidates sometimes underestimate the multi-step democratic hurdle in section 8(1).
questions.mnemonic: New State: two-thirds request, two-thirds local vote, majority of States, two-thirds NASS.

askPresets.answer: Section 8(1) sets four tough stages to create a new State: (a) two-thirds request from NASS, State Assembly, and LGCs of the area; (b) two-thirds referendum approval in the area; (c) simple majority approval across all States of the Federation; and (d) two-thirds resolution of each House of the National Assembly.
State creation requires legislative and popular steps ending in National Assembly resolutions and an Act, never a solo proclamation.

questions.subject: government
questions.topic: Federalism in Nigeria and national unity
questions.stem: What is the primary constitutional goal of the Federal Character Principle stated in section 14(3) of the 1999 Constitution?

options.text: To limit civil service recruitment to Abuja residents only
options.why: Restricting jobs to Abuja residents would defeat federal diversity.
options.whyWrong: Restricting jobs to Abuja residents would defeat federal diversity.

options.text: To abolish all State Governments in favour of one unitary ministry
options.why: Federal Character presupposes a federal system of diverse States, not abolishing States.
options.whyWrong: Federal Character presupposes a federal system of diverse States, not abolishing States.

options.text: To ensure no predominance of persons from a few States or ethnic or sectional groups in the Federal Government and its agencies
options.why: Section 14(3) mandates reflecting Nigeria's federal character to promote national unity and ensure no predominance of persons from a few States or ethnic/sectional groups.

options.text: To replace merit-based judicial trials with quota juries
options.why: Section 14(3) governs composition of government and agencies, not trial verdicts.
options.whyWrong: Section 14(3) governs composition of government and agencies, not trial verdicts.

questions.hint: Remember why Nigeria pairs federalism with representation across all States.
questions.explanation: Section 14(3) (enforced with the Federal Character Commission in the Third Schedule Part I Item C) ensures federal government and agency appointments reflect Nigeria's diversity, preventing dominance by a few States or ethnic/sectional groups; s. 14(4) requires similar inclusivity inside States and LGAs.
questions.trap: Candidates occasionally reduce Federal Character to Abuja residency rather than nationwide inclusion across States and groups.
questions.mnemonic: Federal Character prevents dominance by a few States or groups.

askPresets.answer: Section 14(3) (enforced with the Federal Character Commission in the Third Schedule Part I Item C) ensures federal government and agency appointments reflect Nigeria's diversity, preventing dominance by a few States or ethnic/sectional groups; s. 14(4) requires similar inclusivity inside States and LGAs.
Restricting jobs to Abuja residents would defeat federal diversity.

questions.stem: Under section 162(2) of the 1999 Constitution, when the National Assembly approves a revenue-allocation formula from the Federation Account (upon presidential proposals advised by RMAFC), what minimum derivation percentage must be constantly reflected?

options.text: Not less than 5%
options.why: 5% is below the constitutional floor in s. 162(2).
options.whyWrong: 5% is below the constitutional floor in s. 162(2).

options.text: Not less than 13% of revenue accruing directly from any natural resources
options.why: The proviso to s. 162(2) mandates not less than 13% derivation on revenue accruing to the Federation Account directly from natural resources.

options.text: Not less than 25% of all Value Added Tax
options.why: 25% is the electoral spread threshold, not the s. 162(2) derivation floor.
options.whyWrong: 25% is the electoral spread threshold, not the s. 162(2) derivation floor.

options.text: Not less than 50% of personal income tax
options.why: Section 162(2) sets a 13% floor on natural resources revenue.
options.whyWrong: Section 162(2) sets a 13% floor on natural resources revenue.

questions.hint: Recall the exact percentage written in the proviso to section 162(2).
questions.explanation: Section 162(2) directs the National Assembly to consider population, equality of States, internal revenue generation, landmass, terrain, and population density, subject to the proviso guaranteeing not less than 13% derivation for natural resources.
questions.trap: Historical 1960 and 1963 derivation shares or 5% and 10% guesses often distract students from the 1999 Constitution's 13% floor.
questions.mnemonic: 13% minimum derivation on natural resources in s. 162(2).

options.text: personnel of the Armed Forces, Nigeria Police Force, Foreign Affairs department, and residents of the FCT, Abuja

options.text: There is a single Nigeria Police Force for the Federation, and no other police force may be established for any part of it

questions.stem: Section 7(1) of the 1999 Constitution guarantees a system of local government by

options.text: caretaker committees appointed indefinitely by State Governors

questions.stem: Under section 8(3) and (5)–(6) of the 1999 Constitution, after a State House of Assembly passes a bill creating a new Local Government Area, what is required before it becomes listed in the First Schedule?

options.why: Neighbouring Governors have no constitutional role in creating an LGA inside a State.

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Under section 162(5)–(7) of the 1999 Constitution, how are allocations to local government councils from the Federation Account and State revenue channelled?

options.text: Directly into each council chairman's personal bank account
options.why: Public allocations go into statutory institutional accounts, never personal accounts.
options.whyWrong: Public allocations go into statutory institutional accounts, never personal accounts.

options.text: Through a special State account called the State Joint Local Government Account
options.why: Section 162(6) requires each State to maintain 'the State Joint Local Government Account' into which all Federation Account and State allocations to its local councils are paid.

options.text: Through the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs
options.why: Foreign Affairs plays no role in domestic fiscal transfers.
options.whyWrong: Foreign Affairs plays no role in domestic fiscal transfers.

options.text: Solely from voluntary market donations
options.why: Local councils receive statutory allocations from both the Federation Account (s. 7(6)(a)) and State total revenue (ss. 7(6)(b), 162(7)).
options.whyWrong: Local councils receive statutory allocations from both the Federation Account (s. 7(6)(a)) and State total revenue (ss. 7(6)(b), 162(7)).

questions.hint: Recall the exact name of the special account created by section 162(6).
questions.explanation: Under section 162(5)–(7), allocations standing to local councils in the Federation Account and the prescribed proportion of each State's total revenue are paid into 'the State Joint Local Government Account' maintained by each State for its local councils.
questions.trap: Students know local councils receive federal and state funds yet often forget the exact name in section 162(6).
questions.mnemonic: Section 162(6) creates the State Joint Local Government Account.

askPresets.answer: Under section 162(5)–(7), allocations standing to local councils in the Federation Account and the prescribed proportion of each State's total revenue are paid into 'the State Joint Local Government Account' maintained by each State for its local councils.
Local councils receive statutory allocations from both the Federation Account (s. 7(6)(a)) and State total revenue (ss. 7(6)(b), 162(7)).

questions.subject: government
questions.stem: Which set of duties belongs directly to a Local Government Council under paragraph 1 of the Fourth Schedule to the 1999 Constitution?

options.text: Hearing appeals from Federal High Courts
options.why: Appeals from Federal High Courts go to the Court of Appeal, never local councils.
options.whyWrong: Appeals from Federal High Courts go to the Court of Appeal, never local councils.

options.text: Issuing international passports, controlling airspace, and minting coins
options.why: Immigration/passports, aviation, and currency belong to the Exclusive Legislative List.
options.whyWrong: Immigration/passports, aviation, and currency belong to the Exclusive Legislative List.

options.text: Conducting national population censuses and commanding naval vessels
options.why: Census and defence sit on the Exclusive Legislative List.
options.whyWrong: Census and defence sit on the Exclusive Legislative List.

options.text: Markets, motor parks, cemeteries, naming of roads and streets, and registration of all births, deaths and marriages
options.why: Paragraph 1(c), (e), (g), and (i) of the Fourth Schedule assign cemeteries, markets, motor parks, street naming/house numbering, and registration of births, deaths, and marriages to local councils.

questions.hint: Pick the everyday grassroots community services listed in the Fourth Schedule.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 of the Fourth Schedule assigns local councils local duties including rate collection, cemeteries, bicycle/cart licences, markets and motor parks, local roads/drains, street naming, refuse disposal, outdoor advertising, and birth/death/marriage registration.
questions.trap: Note that while the National Population Commission oversees universal vital registration nationally (3rd Sched.), Fourth Schedule para. 1(i) specifically places local birth, death, and marriage registration in local council duties.
questions.mnemonic: Fourth Schedule = markets, motor parks, cemeteries, street names, vital records.

askPresets.answer: Paragraph 1 of the Fourth Schedule assigns local councils local duties including rate collection, cemeteries, bicycle/cart licences, markets and motor parks, local roads/drains, street naming, refuse disposal, outdoor advertising, and birth/death/marriage registration.
Census and defence sit on the Exclusive Legislative List.

questions.subject: government
questions.concept: Participatory duties under Fourth Schedule para. 2
questions.stem: Under paragraph 2 of the Fourth Schedule to the 1999 Constitution, a Local Government Council's functions include *participating* with the State Government in providing and maintaining

options.text: primary, adult and vocational education, non-mineral agricultural development, and health services
options.why: Paragraph 2(a)–(c) specifically lists participation in primary, adult and vocational education; development of agriculture and natural resources (other than mineral exploitation); and health services.

options.text: crude oil mining, nuclear defence, and foreign embassies
options.why: Mines/minerals, defence, and foreign affairs are Exclusive List federal matters; para. 2(b) explicitly excludes mineral exploitation.
options.whyWrong: Mines/minerals, defence, and foreign affairs are Exclusive List federal matters; para. 2(b) explicitly excludes mineral exploitation.

options.text: printing national currency and regulating maritime shipping
options.why: Currency and maritime shipping belong to the Exclusive Legislative List.
options.whyWrong: Currency and maritime shipping belong to the Exclusive Legislative List.

options.text: appointing Supreme Court Justices
options.why: Supreme Court appointments follow section 231 via the NJC, President, and Senate.
options.whyWrong: Supreme Court appointments follow section 231 via the NJC, President, and Senate.

questions.hint: Notice the specific mineral carve-out inside Fourth Schedule paragraph 2(b)!
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 of the Fourth Schedule empowers local government councils to participate in State governance over (a) primary, adult, and vocational education, (b) agriculture and natural resources *other than mineral exploitation*, (c) health services, and (d) other functions conferred by State Law.
questions.trap: The phrase 'natural resources' in para. 2(b) tricks students into forgetting the explicit words 'other than the exploitation of minerals'.
questions.mnemonic: Councils share primary schools, clinics, and farming — never mineral mining.

askPresets.answer: Paragraph 2 of the Fourth Schedule empowers local government councils to participate in State governance over (a) primary, adult, and vocational education, (b) agriculture and natural resources *other than mineral exploitation*, (c) health services, and (d) other functions conferred by State Law.
Mines/minerals, defence, and foreign affairs are Exclusive List federal matters; para. 2(b) explicitly excludes mineral exploitation.
